description.new:
GET / on the merged server is slow: ~2.4s for the default 30d range and ~6.5s for ?days=0 (all time), measured with curl against the Docker container on 127.0.0.1:8787.

Cause is server-side, not SQLite. cProfile of ccreport.server.dashboard.build(conn, 0) against the live /data/server.db (613063 rows, 285069 after dedup) shows 8.8s wall, of which:

- reports.load (src/ccreport/server/reports.py:69) 6.9s -- it fetches every column of every row in range and builds a UsageRecord + MergedRecord per row (285069 calls to _as_merged, 1.4s just there), then sorts them.
- The folds that follow re-walk that list seven times: account report via reports.build, _chart, _tiles, and four _breakdown calls (3.3s across the four). aggregate.TokenCounts.__iadd__ alone is called 1710416 times.

The page never shows an individual record. Every number on it (five tiles, the account column, the daily chart series, and the four breakdown tables) is a sum over some subset of (machine, account, project, model, day, oslo_date). One GROUP BY over those columns, with the same lowest-id-per-(account_uuid, dk) dedup applied in SQL, returns 1129 rows in 1.2s against the same database -- verified by benchmark.

Note: an ad-hoc benchmark left CREATE INDEX idx_srec_ts ON server_records(ts) committed in the live /data/server.db. Either adopt it in db.py's DDL or drop it.

Acceptance criteria:
- dashboard.build folds from grouped SQL rows rather than from a list of MergedRecord, and keeps the same dedup semantics reports.load has (lowest id wins per (account_uuid, dk); a null dk is kept as it stands).
- A result cache keyed on the range and on a stamp that ingest moves, so a second render of an unchanged database does no query.
- ?days=0 renders in about a second cold and effectively instantly warm; the narrower ranges stay under that.
- Every number on the page is unchanged: tiles, account shares, chart series and all four breakdowns must total the same as before.
- Tests under tests/ cover the new query path and the cache invalidation.

description.new:
`ccreport server allow macsetup dogcat py_project_template` fails with `unrecognized arguments: py_project_template`.

Two separate limits in the parser at src/ccreport/ccreport.py:3000-3002 (the `if name in ("allow", "deny")` branch):

1. `project` is a single positional, so only one project can be allowed or denied per invocation.
2. `url` is a required positional, so the URL must be typed even when push.toml names exactly one server. In the failing command above, `macsetup` was swallowed as the URL and `dogcat` as the project.

cmd_server_allow (src/ccreport/ccreport.py:1723) already calls _resolved_projects([args.project]) — a list of one — so the resolve, the set union/difference, the write_server call and the clear_push_state call all take a list unchanged.

Proposed shape:
- Replace the two positionals with one variadic `targets` (nargs="+").
- If targets[0] is a key in push.read_raw(path), it is the URL and the rest are projects.
- Otherwise, if push.toml names exactly one server, use it and treat every target as a project.
- If targets[0] starts with http:// or https:// and is not configured, that is still the unknown-server error it is today (tests/test_push_policy.py::TestAllowDenyCommands::test_an_unknown_server_is_an_error covers it) — do not fall through to treating a URL as a project name.
- Error when no project is left after the URL is consumed, and when several servers are configured and no URL was given (name them).
- Update the two --help strings for the new positional.

Note push.toml is written by `ccreport server connect` and the allow list is read back through push.load_config.

title.new: Server: an Accounts tab that sets a display alias per account

description.new: Screenshots of the dashboard leak the login email: an account renders as its email everywhere (post@rykroken.net). The server needs an /accounts page where each account gets an alias, and every server-rendered view then shows the alias instead. Decision (asked and answered): server-side only. The CLI's own reports and the statusline keep showing the email, and server_records.account_label keeps holding it — this renames what the server draws, it does not redact what it stores. Where the email comes from today: - The push client stamps each record with account_uuid and account_label from AccountTimeline (src/ccreport/accounts.py, called at src/ccreport/push.py:407). The label is the email. - Ingest stores both columns (src/ccreport/server/db.py:76-77). - Two places turn the pair into a display string, and both spell it the same way: src/ccreport/server/reports.py:116 (full record path) and src/ccreport/server/reports.py:213 (grouped path) — `account = account_label or account_uuid`. That single expression is where an alias lookup belongs, so the dashboard and `ccreport --server` inherit it together. - The account is also a filter: reports.py:61-63 matches `account_label = ? OR account_uuid = ?`. An alias typed as a filter should match too. Proposed shape: - New table `account_aliases(account_uuid TEXT PRIMARY KEY, alias TEXT NOT NULL, updated_at REAL NOT NULL)` in db.py's _SCHEMA_SQL, plus a SCHEMA_VERSION bump. - A db.py reader that returns {account_uuid: alias} and a writer that sets or clears one. - reports.py resolves the display name as alias -> account_label -> account_uuid, in both builders. - New page GET /accounts listing every account_uuid seen in server_records with its stored label, its alias, its record count and its total cost, each row a form that POSTs a new alias. Add `Accounts` to the nav in server/templates/base.html. - The page sits behind the network allowlist like every other page (factory.py wires that; ingest stays outside it). - dashboard.cached_build holds one view per range against db.content_stamp — setting an alias must invalidate that cache, or the page keeps drawing the email until the next push. content_stamp (db.py:328) is the hook. Related: ccreport-26kw is unrelated CLI work; this one is server-side only.

title.new: Server UI: delete a token and delete a machine outright

description.new:
The web UI can mint and revoke, and that is all. A machine minted by mistake — http://10.172.1.236:8787/machines/aa — stays in the list forever, and a revoked token stays in its machine's table forever. Both need a delete.

What exists now:
- db.revoke_token (src/ccreport/server/db.py:263) stamps revoked_at; nothing ever removes the row. The button is in server/templates/machine.html and posts to /tokens/{token_hash}/revoke (src/ccreport/server/pages.py:132).
- machine_tokens, server_records and ingest_files all declare `REFERENCES machines(machine_id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, and db.connect sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` (db.py:214), so deleting the machines row already deletes all three. This is why the confirmation matters: a machine with records holds real money.

Decision (asked and answered): one delete removes everything — the machine, its tokens, its ingest_files and every server_record it pushed — behind typing the machine id to confirm.

Proposed shape:
- db.delete_token(conn, token_hash) -> bool, deleting the row rather than stamping it. Keep revoke: revoking is what you do to a machine that is still out there, deleting is what you do to a mistake.
- db.delete_machine(conn, machine_id) -> int, returning the record count it destroyed, letting the cascade do the rest.
- POST /tokens/{token_hash}/delete beside the existing revoke route, and a Delete button in machine.html's token table next to Revoke.
- POST /machines/{machine_id}/delete, guarded by a form field the person must type the machine id into; a mismatch re-renders the page with an error and deletes nothing. Redirect to /machines on success with a line naming what went: "Deleted aa and its 0 records."
- A machine that no longer exists is a 404 on GET /machines/{id} already (pages.py:68-79); after deletion that is the correct state.
- dashboard.cached_build keys on db.content_stamp — deleting records must move that stamp or the dashboard keeps drawing the deleted machine's spend.

Related: ccreport-1fz1 adds an Accounts tab to the same UI; the two touch pages.py and base.html but not the same routes.

description.new:
Today a restricted machine sends each unallowed project under its own salted pseudonym (src/ccreport/push.py:248 `redact`), and the server draws a row per pseudonym with real cost and tokens. The dashboard therefore shows how many private projects exist and what each one costs. That is the leak: the count and the shape of the work.

Wanted: the server renders no unallowed project at all. Every unallowed record folds into ONE bucket per account, named from the account.

Client side (src/ccreport/push.py):
- `redact` sets project=None, sid=None, cwd=None, repo=None for a record whose project is not in `allow`. No per-project pseudonym, no per-session pseudonym.
- `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session` (push.py:227, :238) lose their only caller. The `salt` field in push.toml and the salt written by `ccreport server connect` become dead — decide in the change whether to keep writing it (harmless, and re-adding a pseudonym later needs it) or drop it from the config and from ServerConfig.
- `policy_hash` (push.py:268) must move when this ships, or every already-pushed file keeps its pseudonym rows: the material it hashes is unchanged by a code edit. Add a redaction-shape constant to that material and bump it. Ingest replaces a file's rows wholesale, and a policy change already sets `replace` on every file, so the old pseudonym rows disappear as the re-push walks the corpus. No server-side purge is needed.

Server side (src/ccreport/server/reports.py):
- A record with project NULL renders as the bucket name instead of NULL. Both builders spell the project the same way today — reports.py:116 (full record path) and reports.py:213 (grouped path) — so the fold belongs there, beside the account resolution.
- Assumed name: `<account display>/aggregated`, where the account display is the alias from ccreport-1fz1 when one is set, and the account label or uuid otherwise. So `post@rykroken.net/aggregated` before an alias and `personal/aggregated` after. The other reading of the request — `<account-id>/<alias>-aggregated`, keeping both — is one f-string away if that is what was meant.
- The bucket must group: two unallowed projects on the same account are one row, one project entry in the dashboard breakdown and one entry in `ccreport --server URL project`.
- The server holds no policy, so it cannot tell a NULL project from a restricted machine apart from a NULL from anything else. NULL only ever arrives from redaction today; if that stops being true the bucket needs a marker column instead.

Depends on ccreport-1fz1 for the alias half of the name; ships without it by falling back to account_label.

notes.new:
DECIDED — bucket name (supersedes the assumed name in the description):

  alias set      ->  `<alias>-aggregated`        e.g. `personal-aggregated`
  no alias       ->  `<account label>/aggregated` e.g. `post@rykroken.net/aggregated`

The email appears only while nothing better exists. Setting an alias removes it
from the string entirely, so `post@rykroken.net/personal-aggregated` must never
be rendered — the alias replaces the whole account segment, slash included.
Fall back to the account uuid where a record carries no label.

One row per account in the project breakdown either way.

DECIDED — salt: keep it. `ccreport server connect` still generates and writes
it, `ServerConfig.salt` stays, and it stays in the policy_hash material, with no
caller once `redact` stops pseudonymizing. `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session`
stay in push.py unused, so re-introducing a pseudonym later needs no config
migration. Because the salt no longer changes when the redaction shape does, the
redaction-shape constant in the policy_hash material is what forces the
re-push — it is not optional.

Sessions are not exempt: sid goes to NULL with project, cwd and repo. A session
count per bucket is itself a signal about the hidden work.

acceptance.new:
- A shared migration runner exists, with steps declared as an ordered numbered list per
  database, and a gap or duplicate version raises at load rather than skipping a step.
- Each step and its version bump commit atomically; a crash mid-step leaves the DB on
  either the old or the new version, never between.
- An applied version whose step has since changed is detected and refuses to run
  further, naming the version.
- Concurrent processes cannot both apply the same step (file lock beside the DB file,
  with a bounded wait that raises rather than hanging).
- server/db.py routes schema changes through the runner; adding a column to
  server_records reaches an existing server database, proven by a test that opens a DB
  at the old schema, adds a step, reopens and asserts the column and the preserved rows.
- cache_db.py's five existing steps are expressed in the new list, and a DB carrying
  the old meta flags does not re-run any of them (test with a pre-seeded meta table).
- just lint-all and just test pass; every new public function has a pytest test.

description.new:
The server database has no migration path. src/ccreport/server/db.py:227 compares
PRAGMA user_version against SCHEMA_VERSION and, when they differ, runs _SCHEMA_SQL --
which is CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS throughout. On an existing server file every one
of those creates is a no-op, so a column added to server_records never appears and
bumping SCHEMA_VERSION changes nothing. The docstring at db.py:21 tells the next agent
to bump it, which reads as a working mechanism and is not one. That file is the only
copy of a machine's records once its JSONL logs have rotated, so the failure mode is a
query against a missing column on a database nothing can rebuild.

cache.db does migrate, ad hoc: _ADDED_COLUMNS (cache_db.py:379) for plain ADD COLUMN,
plus five meta-flagged steps in _run_migrations (cache_db.py:607-781). Each step
hand-rolls its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE, rollback handler and post-hoc verification, and
the flag write is what makes it once-only. It works; it is copy-pasted per step and
has no ordering, no log and no guard against an edited step.

Reference implementation studied: /Users/ove/Trash/migrate (src/migra/db/migration/).
Four things there fit ccreport:

1. A numbered chain validated at load -- gaps and duplicate versions are hard errors
   (migrations.py:361, _validate_migrations).
2. The step and its version bump applied in ONE executescript, so a crash cannot land
   between the schema change and the pointer update (migrations.py:480).
3. A migration_checksum table: refuse to start when a version that was already applied
   no longer matches the code that ran (migrations.py:432).
4. An flock file beside the database, taken for the whole run (migrations.py:144).
   ccreport needs this: statusline, push and ccu open cache.db from separate processes
   concurrently, and today two of them can enter the bootstrap at once.

Do NOT copy from it: the .sql-file format (ccreport migrations carry Python logic --
migration 2b at cache_db.py:651 matches model names by substring, which SQL cannot
express), the 1:1 testfile pairing, the symlink/BOM/filename-case hardening (that
guards an operator-supplied directory; ccreport ships its steps in its own package),
or the psqtie DB wrapper.

Shape agreed with the user: one shared module (e.g. src/ccreport/migrations.py) that
both databases call. Steps are Python callables in a numbered list, one list per
database. PRAGMA user_version stays the pointer -- both files already use it. The
existing cache_db meta flags must keep working: a database that already ran
migrated_dedup_keys_pk_order must not re-run it as step N.

Constraint from AGENTS.md: statusline.py imports nothing outside the stdlib and defers
cache_db into the functions that touch the DB. The new module is imported by cache_db,
not by statusline, and everything it does stays behind the user_version gate so a warm
render pays nothing.

- An applied version whose step source or name has since changed is detected and
  refuses to run further, naming the version.
- Concurrent processes cannot both apply the same step (file lock beside the DB file,
  with a bounded wait that raises rather than hanging).
- server/db.py routes schema changes through the runner; adding a column to
  server_records reaches an existing server database, proven by a test that opens a DB
  at the old schema, adds a step, reopens and asserts the column and the preserved rows.
- cache_db.py routes schema changes through the runner above baseline 11. The frozen
  pre-baseline bootstrap still runs for a database below it, and a database carrying
  the old meta flags re-runs none of the five legacy steps (test with a pre-seeded
  meta table).
- SCHEMA_VERSION in both files is derived from the chain head, not hand-edited, and a
  test fails if either is set independently.
- just lint-all and just test pass; every new public function has a pytest test.

DESIGN (agreed with the user before implementation)

Module: src/ccreport/migrations.py. Stdlib only. Imported by cache_db.py and
server/db.py, never by statusline.py, and reached only behind the user_version gate.

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class Step:
        version: int
        name: str
        apply: Callable[[sqlite3.Connection], None] | None   # None = version bump only
        legacy_flag: str | None = None

    def run(conn, *, chain, baseline, db_path, applied_flags=None) -> int

Log table, created by run() in both databases before the first step:

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
        version    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        name       TEXT NOT NULL,
        applied_at REAL NOT NULL,
        source_sha TEXT
    );

Per step: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, apply(conn), insert the log row, PRAGMA user_version = N,
COMMIT. user_version is header state and is transactional, so no executescript splice
is needed to keep the bump with the DDL. The restriction that buys: a step runs inside
a transaction, where PRAGMA foreign_keys is a no-op, so a table rebuild must tolerate
FK enforcement staying on -- which the existing dedup_keys rebuild at cache_db.py:738
already does. A step that genuinely cannot is out of scope until one exists.

SCHEMA_VERSION stops being hand-edited in both files: it becomes chain[-1].version. A
change that only adds a table still needs a chain entry, with apply=None, to move the
version and so re-run _SCHEMA_SQL.

Numbering: continue from the current stamp. cache.db baseline is 11 and the server
baseline is 3. _SCHEMA_SQL, _ADDED_COLUMNS and the five meta-flagged steps in
_run_migrations are the frozen pre-baseline bootstrap and are NOT re-expressed as chain
entries -- a database below its baseline takes the legacy path and is then treated as
sitting at the baseline. New steps start at 12 (cache.db) and 4 (server). The rejected
alternative renumbered from 1 with each meta key as a legacy_flag skip-guard; it needs
a user_version-to-chain mapping, and one wrong entry re-runs a data migration against a
live cache.

Validation at load: versions strictly ascending by one from baseline + 1, no
duplicates, and a database whose user_version exceeds the head raises rather than
being silently downgraded.

Lock: <db_path>.migration-lock, opened O_CREAT|O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW at 0600, flock
LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB polled to a 60 s deadline, released after the last step. fcntl is
POSIX-only, matching this project's darwin/linux targets.

Drift guard: source_sha is sha256 over inspect.getsource(step.apply), recorded on apply
and compared on later opens. Unreadable source records NULL and is compared against
nothing. A recorded name that no longer matches the chain entry raises regardless.
inspect is imported on the migration path only.

description.new:
Claude Code fires a ConfigChange hook when a settings file changes (user, project, local, policy) or a skills file changes. The payload carries session_id, transcript_path, cwd, config_source and config_path. Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#configchange

The status line caches its fetch results per session for FAST_TTL_S (15 s) in $TMPDIR/claude-statusline-<uid>-<sid>.json (statusline._fast_cache_path). Two of the cached values are read out of settings files: the sbx/!sbx badge, which walks local -> project -> user settings in statusline._render_sandbox (src/ccreport/statusline.py:1189), and the CLAUDE_CODE_STATUSLINE_* segment toggles that settings 'env' feeds. After an edit they stay stale for up to 15 s.

Wire a ConfigChange hook that deletes that file, so the next render takes the slow path and re-reads the settings. The memo file (.memo.json) is not touched: its DSP verdict comes from the claude process argv and its ~/.claude.json stamp is invalidated by that file's own mtime/size.

Model it on bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh: read stdin, jq the session_id, sanitize it the same way _session_state_path does, rm -f, print nothing, exit 0 on every path. Exit 0 matters twice over here — a ConfigChange hook that exits 2 blocks the config change from taking effect.

Also add a README section covering both status line hooks (the existing SessionStart memo one and this one), and wire the hook into ~/git/macsetup/claude/mbp2022/settings.json and ~/git/macsetup/claude/sbnorge/settings.json.

description.new:
The Dockerfile's CMD is development-shaped and cannot be published as-is. It ends in:

    CMD ["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--reload"]

`--reload` starts a watchfiles reloader over a bind mount a published image does not have (src/ccreport/server/fastapi_server.py:33). It also silently forces workers to 1 (same file, line 33: `workers=1 if args.reload else args.workers`), which is what one SQLite file wants — so today the correct worker count is an accident of the reload flag.

Changes:
1. `Dockerfile`: CMD becomes `["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--workers", "1"]`. --workers 1 is explicit because the argparse default is 2 (fastapi_server.py:48).
2. `docker-compose.yml`: add a `command:` on the ccreport-server service carrying the --reload form, so `just docker-up` keeps the behaviour its own comments describe and the read-only ./src mount stays useful.
3. `tests/test_docker_image.py`: new test in the spirit of tests/test_dashboard.py's remote-origin guard. Parse both files and assert the image CMD carries --workers 1 and no --reload, and the compose command carries --reload. They are a pair; an edit to one alone either ships a reloading server or breaks local development with no failing test.

This blocks the release workflow — a tag must not publish a reloading image.

title: Split the Dockerfile CMD from docker-compose's dev command

description.new:
The server image exists only on the machine that built it. Give it a named, reproducible artifact on GHCR, cut from a tag.

File to create: `.github/workflows/release-server.yml`

- Trigger: `push: tags: ['server-v*']`. The prefix keeps server versions clear of the CLI's commit-count model — the CLI has no tags and is not affected.
- `permissions: contents: write, packages: write`.
- Two jobs. A `test` job repeating the CI steps (uv sync --group dev, just lint-all, pytest), and an `image` job with `needs: test`, so a tag cannot ship an untested tree.
- image job: docker/setup-qemu-action, docker/setup-buildx-action, docker/login-action against ghcr.io with secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN, then docker/build-push-action with `platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64`.
- Tags: `ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${VERSION}` and `:latest`, where VERSION is GITHUB_REF_NAME with the `server-v` prefix stripped. github.repository is oroddlokken/ccreport, already lowercase, so no case fix is needed.
- docker/metadata-action supplies the OCI labels so the image records its version and revision.
- Final step: softprops/action-gh-release for the tag with `generate_release_notes: true`. This repo has no CHANGELOG.md, unlike dogcat — do not port dogcat's awk extraction.
- Pin every action by commit SHA.

The arm64 leg runs under QEMU and downloads rather than compiles: uv.lock carries musllinux aarch64 wheels for granian, watchfiles, orjson, pydantic-core and markupsafe, and the base is ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-alpine.

Model: https://github.com/kluzzebass/gastrolog/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml (QEMU + buildx + GHCR multi-arch). Its scratch-image and homebrew jobs do not apply here.

Out of scope: the sea deployment. It keeps pulling the ccreport_server branch through the $INFRA_DIR playbook, and .deploy.remote.settings.toml is not edited.

- A reading older than the staleness budget, or no reading at all, blocks, and
  the stopReason names the environment variable to unset.
- Tests cover each verdict against the existing SQLite fixtures.

description.new:
A quota guard that stops a session before it crosses into extra usage, so an
org account never pays for overflow it did not choose.

Armed by environment only: `CCQUOTA_STOP` unset makes both hooks exit 0 before
they touch Python, so an unarmed session pays one bash spawn per prompt.
`CCQUOTA_WARN=85 CCQUOTA_STOP=95 claude` arms one session; the environment is
read at launch, so a launcher alias is how it gets used in practice.

Hook input carries no quota data — only session_id, transcript_path, cwd,
permission_mode, hook_event_name and effort. The readings come from the local
cache instead: the statusline writes `five_hour` and `seven_day` to
rate_limit_snapshots from Claude Code's own stdin on every render, and the
usage row holds sonnet_percent and scoped_percent from the 10-minute API fetch.

Two hooks, one shared verdict module:

- UserPromptSubmit: over the warn line emits systemMessage; over the stop line
  emits `{"continue": false, "stopReason": ...}`, which halts processing and
  leaves the session open for input.
- PreToolUse: same verdict, so a turn already running halts at its next tool
  call rather than burning to the end of the window.

No hook can exit the CLI. `continue: false` is the strongest stop the harness
offers, and stopReason reaches the person, never Claude.

Fail-closed on an unknown reading, with two distinctions that decide whether
the guard is usable:

- A quota the API nulls because the plan does not have it (see the
  _API_QUOTA_FIELDS comment in usage_api.py) is not applicable, not unknown.
  Conflating them blocks the first prompt of every plan without a Sonnet cap.
- Unknown carries an age. The fetch TTL is 600s, so a reading younger than ~15
  minutes counts and anything older or absent blocks. Say so in the stopReason:
  the way out is unsetting the variable and restarting.

Warnings dedupe on the window instance. Key a TMPDIR memo on resets_at, the
same shape bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh already uses, so one warning lands per
window and a fresh one lands after the window rolls.

Scope note: the quota is per account, not per session. This stops the sessions
that carry the variable on this machine, and nothing else.

description.old:
The Dockerfile's CMD is development-shaped and cannot be published as-is. It ends in:

    CMD ["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--reload"]

`--reload` starts a watchfiles reloader over a bind mount a published image does not have (src/ccreport/server/fastapi_server.py:33). It also silently forces workers to 1 (same file, line 33: `workers=1 if args.reload else args.workers`), which is what one SQLite file wants — so today the correct worker count is an accident of the reload flag.

Changes:
1. `Dockerfile`: CMD becomes `["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--workers", "1"]`. --workers 1 is explicit because the argparse default is 2 (fastapi_server.py:48).
2. `docker-compose.yml`: add a `command:` on the ccreport-server service carrying the --reload form, so `just docker-up` keeps the behaviour its own comments describe and the read-only ./src mount stays useful.
3. `tests/test_docker_image.py`: new test in the spirit of tests/test_dashboard.py's remote-origin guard. Parse both files and assert the image CMD carries --workers 1 and no --reload, and the compose command carries --reload. They are a pair; an edit to one alone either ships a reloading server or breaks local development with no failing test.

This blocks the release workflow — a tag must not publish a reloading image.

description.old:
The server image exists only on the machine that built it. Give it a named, reproducible artifact on GHCR, cut from a tag.

File to create: `.github/workflows/release-server.yml`

- Trigger: `push: tags: ['server-v*']`. The prefix keeps server versions clear of the CLI's commit-count model — the CLI has no tags and is not affected.
- `permissions: contents: write, packages: write`.

- Final step: softprops/action-gh-release for the tag with `generate_release_notes: true`. This repo has no CHANGELOG.md, unlike dogcat — do not port dogcat's awk extraction.
- Pin every action by commit SHA.

The arm64 leg runs under QEMU and downloads rather than compiles: uv.lock carries musllinux aarch64 wheels for granian, watchfiles, orjson, pydantic-core and markupsafe, and the base is ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-alpine.

description.new:
No test parses a Claude Code session log. The suite seeds cache.db directly with fabricated file paths (tests/test_cache_db.py, tests/report_fixture.py), and test_forecast.py keeps its subject off the real ~/.claude/projects. `parse_jsonl_file` in src/ccreport/ccreport.py is the front of the whole pipeline and has no end-to-end coverage, so nobody knows whether `just test` passes on a machine that has never run Claude Code. A GitHub runner is exactly that machine, which is why this blocks ccreport-25in: a red first CI run would not say whether the workflow or the suite is wrong.

Add `tools/make_synthetic_logs.py`, alongside the existing tools/ scripts:

- Takes an output directory and writes a projects/ tree of JSONL session logs into it — several projects, several sessions each, more than one model, and enough days for a report to have rows to group.
- Derive the record shape from `parse_jsonl_file` and the JSONL fields it actually reads, not from memory of Claude Code's format. A generator that writes fields the reader ignores proves nothing.
- Runnable by hand for reproducing a parse bug outside pytest, and importable so a test can build a corpus into tmp_path.
- Nothing is committed as data. The corpus is generated per run; only the script lives in the repo.

Then at least one test that points the reader at a generated tree and asserts what comes back: token counts, model, session and project per record.

notes.new:
Built as src/ccreport/quota_guard.py plus bin/quota-guard.sh, wired to both events by one wrapper. Two departures from the issue text, both agreed with the user first:

1. Freshness for S and W comes from a new per-session TMPDIR file (.quota) that statusline._save_quota_reading writes on slow renders while CCQUOTA_STOP is set. rate_limit_snapshots writes a row only when a reading moves a whole percent, so its newest ts dates the last change, not the last observation, and a quiet session would have read as stale at any quota level. Snapshots and the usage row remain fallbacks.
2. Staleness is per source: NATIVE_MAX_AGE_S 900s for the stdin reading, API_MAX_AGE_S 3600s for Sonnet and scoped. The 600s fetch TTL is not the ceiling on the usage row's age - statusline.USAGE_HEARTBEAT_S is, since a render skips the API while nothing on the line needs it.

Tests: tests/test_quota_guard.py, 58 cases. Full suite 1742 passed, just lint-all clean. README has a 'The quota guard' section; AGENTS.md has the module entry and a pipeline rule.

description.new:
A slow render whose cost summary has aged past COST_SUMMARY_MAX_AGE (900 s) re-reads the project's JSONL logs on the render thread, in the frame Claude Code is waiting on.

Path: src/ccreport/statusline.py:2030 -> src/ccreport/pricing.py:1383 (compute_project_rolling_costs).

Measured on an 8 GB A18 Pro (2 performance cores, fanless): the walk takes 0.566 s cold against a 0.08 s full render, measured with

    python3 -c "import sys,time; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from ccreport.pricing import compute_project_rolling_costs as f; t=time.monotonic(); f('$PWD'); print(time.monotonic()-t)"
    just bench

0.566 s is a floor, not a worst case: it ran directly after 'ccreport --json' had refreshed the record cache. This project is 73 MB across 98 .jsonl files; the largest single log on the machine is 54.8 MB. The record cache is refreshed by CLI runs alone, so an active session's log never matches cached_meta and always takes the full-parse branch.

The cadence is worse than once per 900 s. When is_costs_refresh_blocked() suppresses the detached --costs-only spawn (src/ccreport/statusline.py:748), the summary is never rewritten while the inline walk still runs, so a project that loses the machine-wide costs lock pays this every slow render.

Chosen approach: render the previous cycle's project costs, already held in _Fetched, and pick up the fresh summary on the next render - what the 15 s fast cache already does for every other slow value. Costs land one render behind rather than stale.

Rejected: widening COST_SUMMARY_MAX_AGE. That leaves the cost windows stale instead of one render behind.

The project cost segment shows the previous cycle's figure on that render and the fresh one on the next. 'just bench' shows no regression in phase 1 wall time. Tests under tests/test_statusline.py cover the expired-summary path and assert no inline walk.

title.new: Thin cache.db snapshots to weekly past the recent few days

acceptance.new: Retention keeps N recent dailies and one per week beyond them, configurable through the existing CLAUDE_CACHE_SNAPSHOT_KEEP and a new weekly bound. The pre-bootstrap copy and _sanity_check are untouched. Tests under tests/test_cache_db.py cover the thinning boundary with a fixed clock, including the day a daily becomes the week's keeper.

description.new:
The daily snapshot is a whole-file copy of a database that only grows, and retention is counted in files rather than bytes.

Path: src/ccreport/cache_db.py:993 (_maybe_snapshot), :37 (_SNAPSHOT_KEEP_DEFAULT = 14), :36 (_DEFAULT_SNAPSHOT_DIR).

Measured on this machine: ~/.local/share/ccreport/snapshots holds 1.8 GB, one 155.7 MB .db per day, 14 kept. The copy alone writes ~57 GB/year to a soldered SSD. Both figures grow with tables the schema comments describe as never pruned - ccreport_records ('only ever grows'), rate_limit_snapshots ('Never pruned'), exchange_rates ('never pruned').

The render does not take the copy itself: src/ccreport/statusline.py:2525 sets CLAUDE_CACHE_SNAPSHOT_DEFER=1, so the detached refresh does. The write still happens once a day.

Chosen approach: keep the last few days daily, then thin older snapshots to weekly, in _maybe_snapshot's retention step.

Do not disable the pre-bootstrap copy. get_connection takes it as the pre-image for the only code that rewrites existing rows, and _sanity_check compares against it.

CLAUDE_CACHE_SNAPSHOT_KEEP is a per-machine workaround for the resident 1.8 GB, but it does not change the daily 155.7 MB write.

title: Thin cache.db snapshots to weekly past the recent few days

description.new:
The PreToolUse hook fires before every tool call, and past the CCQUOTA_STOP gate each one starts a CPython interpreter, opens cache.db and runs nine queries.

Paths: bin/quota-guard.sh:9 (the CCQUOTA_STOP gate is the only early exit), src/ccreport/quota_guard.py:182, :241 (four separate 'ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1' queries against rate_limit_snapshots, one per window).

Measured on an 8 GB A18 Pro (2 performance cores, fanless): 39.3 ms wall and 25.6 ms user CPU per invocation, over 100 runs:

    time (for i in $(seq 1 100); do CCQUOTA_STOP=99 bash bin/quota-guard.sh <<< '{"session_id":"probe"}' >/dev/null; done)

The multiplier - tool calls per agentic turn - is not measured. On a fanless chassis this is a sustained-load cost, not a peak one.

Chosen approach: replace the four per-window queries with one grouped statement.

description.new:
Snapshots are stored as whole, uncompressed SQLite files: ~/.local/share/ccreport/snapshots holds 1.8 GB, one 163.3 MB .db per day, 14 kept. SQLite pages compress about ten to one, so compressing the rotated ones cuts the resident bytes by roughly that factor.

Measured on 2026-08-15.db (163,266,560 bytes) on this machine:
  stdlib lzma, preset 1 - 16,364,208 bytes, 1.8 s
  zstd -3 -T0           - 18,898,765 bytes
  gzip -6               - 21,560,638 bytes, 1.2 s

lzma wins on ratio and ships with Python, so there is no reason to probe for an installed zstd or xz binary and no subprocess. Python 3.13 has no stdlib zstd; compression.zstd lands in 3.14, and pyproject requires-python is >=3.13.

Path: src/ccreport/cache_db.py:1037 (the rotation step in _maybe_snapshot), :1125 and :1131 (_sanity_check's glob and read-only open), :1096 (the restore hint).

Two constraints on where the compression goes.

1. The newest snapshot from a prior day has to stay a plain .db. _sanity_check opens it read-only at :1131 for the ccreport_records counts, and _warn_on_drop prints 'Restore with: cp <snapshot> <DB_PATH>' at :1096. Decompressing 163 MB to run two COUNT(*) queries would put that cost on every migrate run and every day's snapshot run.

2. Compress during rotation, not at write time. conn.backup already writes the full 163 MB; compressing in the same pass adds a 163 MB read plus a 16 MB write to that day. Compressing a file that is already days old moves the work off the write path and touches each file once.

This is separate from ccreport-2bbk (thin snapshots to weekly) and multiplies with it: thinning alone still keeps the same number of files, just spread over more days, so it widens coverage rather than cutting the 1.8 GB. Neither change cuts the daily 163 MB write - only not copying every day would.

Adjacent, in the same rotation step: the glob '????-??-??.db' at :1038 unlinks the .db and leaves the -shm and -wal sidecars a read-only connection created beside it. 11 orphans at 32K each are in the directory now, the oldest for 2026-07-06, whose .db has already been rotated away. Whatever the compressed extension is, the rotation and the glob in _sanity_check both need to know about it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Snapshots older than the plain-file window are stored compressed with stdlib lzma; the newest prior-day snapshot stays a readable .db.
- _sanity_check picks the newest prior-day plain .db and never decompresses.
- Rotation counts compressed and plain snapshots as one series, and removes the -shm and -wal sidecars along with the .db.
- The restore hint names a command that works for the file it points at.
- Tests under tests/test_cache_db.py cover the rotation boundary with a fixed clock: the day a plain snapshot becomes a compressed one, and a directory holding both kinds.

description.new:
The push interval is fixed at 30 minutes: push.py:35 `BASE_INTERVAL_S = 30 * 60`. A fast machine on a wired network can push every 5 minutes and keep the merged view fresh; a mobile machine on a metered link wants 15 minutes or more. The interval is a property of the machine and its link, not of the server, so it belongs in that machine's push.toml entry beside `networks` and `max_body`.

Add a per-server field (suggested `interval_minutes`, an int) to `[server."URL"]`:

- `ServerConfig` (push.py:61) gains the field; `load_config` (push.py:139) parses it, falling back to `BASE_INTERVAL_S` when absent or unparseable. `write_server` and `_toml_value` (push.py:185, 210) already handle ints.
- `due()` (push.py:571) and `next_attempt_at()` (push.py:648) each recompute `min(BASE_INTERVAL_S * (2 ** failures), MAX_INTERVAL_S)` inline. Both must use the configured base, so factor the doubling into one helper both call.
- `MAX_INTERVAL_S` (8 h) is the failure-widening ceiling. A configured base above it must not be clamped below itself: the ceiling is `max(MAX_INTERVAL_S, base)`.
- Give `ccreport server connect` a flag that writes it (cmd_server_connect, ccreport.py:1363; its parser, ccreport.py:2706) so nobody has to hand-edit a 0600 file, and print the interval in `ccreport server status` (ccreport.py:1463) beside `network gate`.

AGENTS.md lists push.toml's keys as "server, token, restricted, allow, salt, networks"; add the new one there.

description.new:
A ccreport server is a terminal today: machines push to it and nothing leaves. This epic adds a second service that several ccreport servers push aggregated totals to, and that ranks those servers by spend.

What crosses the wire: one row per (day, model) carrying input, output, cache-creation and cache-read tokens plus a call count. No project, session, machine, account, cwd or repo. The pushing server's owner types a handle when the token is minted, because nothing in the payload can derive one.

Decisions taken with the user on 2026-08-16:
- Ranking is raw spend, not an efficiency measure.
- One row per pushing server, not per account. A shared server's users stay merged, which also raises the re-identification floor.
- The board is a separate service: its own package, database, migration chain and entry point, living in this repo beside src/ccreport/server/.

Cross-cutting design points the children carry:
- The board prices the counts with its own pricing.py, so one price table ranks every participant and a client with a stale table cannot distort the order.
- A machine pushes old logs late, so a day already sent changes afterwards. Ingest upserts (handle, day, model) rather than appending, and the push watermark is a content stamp rather than a max timestamp.
- day is the pushing machine's calendar day, carried through server_records. The board stores it as received and never re-derives it from an instant.
- Nothing audits the counts. A token proves which server sent a row and no more, so the board shows a handle's join date and day count beside its total.

title.new: Prune untiered rate-limit windows in a one-time migration

description.new:
`ccreport limits` shows window instances whose Tier column reads as absent: their first sample predates the account_events tier columns, so nothing recorded what the account was entitled to while the window filled. Six session windows, one week window and one scoped window on this machine (2026-08-08 through 2026-08-09). They carry a peak and a spend but no tier, which makes them unusable for the comparison the report exists for.

Remove them from the data rather than from the renderer: append a numbered Step to MIGRATION_CHAIN in src/ccreport/cache_db.py (version 12, MIGRATION_BASELINE is 11) that deletes every rate_limit_snapshots row belonging to an instance whose earliest sample resolves to no effective tier.

- An instance is (window, model, resets_at); the tier is attributed at its earliest ts, the same rule report_limits uses (src/ccreport/ccreport.py:2469).
- The tier in force at a ts is the newest account_events row at or before it, through cache_db.effective_limit_tier (user tier over org tier).
- The rate_limit_snapshots comment at src/ccreport/cache_db.py:318 says the table is never pruned; amend it to name this step.
- Hazard to state in the code: a machine whose account_events rows are all pre-tier loses its whole snapshot history, and a sample is unreconstructible once dropped.

acceptance.new:
- Step(12, ...) appended to MIGRATION_CHAIN; SCHEMA_VERSION derives to 12 with no hand edit
- A DB whose snapshots are all untiered ends with an empty rate_limit_snapshots; one with a mix keeps exactly the tiered instances, all samples of each
- An instance straddling the first tiered account_event is judged by its earliest sample alone
- Re-running the step is a no-op (the version stamp is the flag)
- pytest coverage under tests/ for: mixed DB, all-untiered DB, empty account_events, and the straddling case
- just lint-all and just test pass

description.new:
The caption under each limits table reads as shorthand nobody can decode:

  open at 10.0% (2026-08-17 11:56), seen from 0.0%; 38.8 pp/h → 193% by reset 2026-08-17 16:40; 90.0 pp left ≈ $91
  open at 1.0% (2026-08-17 11:46), seen from 0.0%; 10.3 pp/h → 1595% by reset 2026-08-23 22:00; 99.0 pp left ≈ $362

Two faults. The wording is jargon (pp/h, 'seen from', a percentage past 100 where the point is a clock time), and the second line projects a 7-day window from five minutes of watching, which is where 1595% comes from.

Approved shape, one sentence per open window:

  Session, still open: 10% used at 11:56, from 0% when first seen. Filling 39% an hour — at that rate it hits the limit about 14:20, before the 16:40 reset. The 90% left is worth about $91.
  Week, still open: 1% used at 11:46, from 0% when first seen. Too little watched yet to project. The 99% left is worth about $362.

- The whole caption is ccreport._open_note (src/ccreport/ccreport.py); the arithmetic is WindowInstance.projected_pct.
- A projection at or past 100 prints the hour the window hits the limit instead of the percentage. That hour is the inverse of projected_pct: last_ts + (100 - latest_pct) / burn_pph.
- A window watched for less than 5% of its span (15 min of a session, 8.4 h of a week, from _LIMIT_WINDOW_SPAN_S) prints no projection at all. A type with no known span keeps projecting — there is nothing to measure the span against.
- Percentages read as whole numbers in a sentence, tenths only below 1%. A moment on today's date reads as the clock alone, any other day carries its date.
- A scoped window opens the sentence with its model name, the way it does now; the others open with the window name off _LIMIT_WINDOW_LABELS, so nothing spells 'Session' twice.

description.new:
compute_costs can return a 24h window larger than all_time for the same corpus, when a cached record carries a stored cost that differs from what its tokens price.

Where: src/ccreport/pricing.py:1483, inside _try_cached_file branch 3 (the branch for a file whose file_costs fingerprint and ccreport_files fingerprint both match). It prices each cached record with _rec_cost(), which returns the record's stored cost whenever that is non-zero and only falls back to tokens otherwise. ccreport_records.cost is the log's costUSD verbatim (scan.py:276), so for a log that carried costUSD the rolling windows are filled from costUSD.

Meanwhile all_time, week and month for that same file come from cached_entry, which compute_costs wrote from _scan_jsonl_file -> _line_cost -> calc_cost, i.e. from tokens. The JSONL parse path never reads costUSD at all.

So one call's result is internally inconsistent, and two calls over an unchanged corpus disagree with each other:

- cold (file_costs empty): every file is scanned, everything priced from tokens
- warm (both caches fresh): all_time from tokens, rolling windows from costUSD

Observed while porting a test in ccreport-4lmq: a four-record project totalled all_time 0.07 and twenty_four_hour 1.035 on the warm call, where the cold call gave 0.07 for both. The fixture's cached records carried cost 0.5 each against tokens worth 0.0175.

Repro sketch (see the fixtures in tests/test_pricing.py TestLiveFilesPricedFromTheCcreportCache): write a JSONL file, save_ccreport_file it with a matching (mtime_ns, size) and a record whose stored cost disagrees with its tokens, call compute_costs(cwd=...) twice, compare.

The now-deleted compute_project_rolling_costs used _rec_cost_from_tokens for exactly this case, with the reason in its own comment: the raw path recomputes, so a file still on disk has nothing to lose by recomputing too. The orphan and purged-session paths (pricing.py:1052, 1152, 1234) must keep _rec_cost - there is no file left to re-price from, so the stored cost is the only surviving figure.

Candidate fix: use _rec_cost_from_tokens at pricing.py:1483. Weigh it first: for a corpus whose logs carry costUSD this moves the printed window figures, and costUSD is arguably the biller's own number. The alternative is to make the scan path prefer costUSD too, which changes far more.

Note pricing.py:1440-ish (_orphan_alltime_fingerprint's docstring) states almost no cached record carries a stored cost at all, which is why this has gone unnoticed - Claude Code's current logs appear not to write costUSD.

docs/calculation-reference.md section 5.6 now states which cost each path uses; update that bullet with whatever this issue decides.

title.new: Warm caches make a rolling window exceed all_time in compute_costs

acceptance.new: compute_costs returns the same figures for an unchanged corpus whether its caches are warm or cold, and no rolling window can exceed all_time. The orphan and purged-session paths still keep the stored cost. docs/calculation-reference.md section 5.6 matches the outcome.

Month and week pages, plus By month and By week breakdowns
description:
The server has /day/2026-07-30 (dashboard.build treats a day scope as its own range, charting by hour). Add the two periods above it:

- GET /month/2026-07 — the calendar month, day axis.
- GET /week/2026-07-30 — the Monday-start week containing that date, day axis. The URL renders in place: a non-Monday date is not redirected, and the header span shows the Mon-Sun span it drew.

Also add month and week as breakdown dimensions, so they appear as dashboard tabs (dashboard.html) and as tables on every detail page, with each row linking to its own page.

Where the work is:
- src/ccreport/server/dashboard.py — DIMENSIONS, SCOPES, _DIMENSION_KEYS (week key = the Monday of the record day_key(), month key = day_key()[:7]), and build(), whose `hourly` branch generalizes to a period branch. A day keeps reports.load and the hour axis; week and month use load_grouped over a window widened a day at each end, then match the period day set afterwards, because `day` is the pushing machine calendar day and a machine on another clock keeps records whose instant falls outside this server day.
- src/ccreport/server/pages.py — the catch-all /{dimension}/{key} validates against dashboard.SCOPES; it must admit the new period scopes and 404 a malformed key (2026-13, 2026-07-32) rather than 500.
- src/ccreport/server/templates/detail.html — the range toggle is hidden for a period scope, not for `day` alone.
- AGENTS.md — the pipeline bullet stating a day page is the one build that calls reports.load needs the period wording.
acceptance: GET /month/2026-07 and /week/2026-07-30 render 200 with four charts over a day axis; the week page covers Mon 2026-07-27 through Sun 2026-08-02. A malformed key is 404. Every scoped page total equals the sum of its own By day rows. The dashboard has month and week tabs whose rows link to the new pages. just lint-all and just test pass, with new tests in tests/test_detail_pages.py.

Cache-hit share per rate-limit window, in the CLI table and on a server page
description:
`ccreport limits` prints Peak, Samples, Fill, pp/h, Spend, $/pp, Extra and Hit
per window instance, and says nothing about how much of the work in that window
was served from the prompt cache. Cache-read tokens are the cheapest tokens on
the corpus, so a window with a high cache-hit share buys more work per rate-limit
point than one without, and $/pp alone cannot show why two windows differ.

The same history has no reader on the ccreport server: rate-limit snapshots are
a client-only table today, so the merged dashboard cannot show window history at
all.

## Scope 1 — CLI

Add a cache-hit column to the three `ccreport limits` tables (session, week,
scoped model) and the matching field to `ccreport limits --json`.

- `WindowSpend` (`src/ccreport/ccreport.py:2153`) carries `usd`, `per_pp`,
  `headroom_usd`, `extra_usd` and nothing token-shaped. The token counts are
  already on the records `_load_instance_spend` (`ccreport.py:2232`) loads:
  `TokenCounts.cache_read` and `.cache_create` in `src/ccreport/aggregate.py:36`.
- Measure it over the fill span (first sample to peak), the span `rise`,
  `burn_pph` and `usd` already share, so the row describes one stretch of time.
- Decide and document which ratio the column prints — cache_read over
  (input + cache_create + cache_read) is the reading that answers "how much of
  this window's context was already paid for". Put the definition in
  `docs/calculation-reference.md` section 9 beside the other window maths.
- `_limits_entry` (`ccreport.py:2335`) gains the raw numbers, not a formatted
  string, per its own docstring.
- A window with no priced records shows the absent marker, the same as Spend.

## Scope 2 — server page

Add a rate-limit window page to the server dashboard showing the same table,
merged across machines, with each window row linking to a page for that one
window instance.

- `rate_limit_snapshots` lives in cache.db alone (`src/ccreport/cache_db.py:329`).
  `push.py` sends `ccreport_records` only (`push.build_files`, `_records_for`,
  `push.py:415`), so this needs a new payload section, a server-side table and
  an ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`.
- Server schema changes go through `migrations.py`: a numbered `Step` appended
  to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in `src/ccreport/server/db.py`, per AGENTS.md.
- Snapshots carry no project and no session, so the restricted-machine
  redaction in `push.redact` has nothing to strip — confirm that reading before
  sending them, and decide whether a restricted machine sends them at all.
- The page belongs with the dashboard, not under `/settings`. Note that
  `/{dimension}/{key}` in `src/ccreport/server/pages.py:329` is the catch-all
  and matches whatever the named routes did not, so a new named route has to be
  registered before it.
- Charts follow the existing rules: fixed series order from
  `server/static/palette.js`, one scale per chart, vendored chart library, and
  assets linked through the `asset()` template global.
- The per-window detail page shows what the CLI's row summarizes plus the
  sample series that produced it: the fill curve over time, the records that
  filled it, and the cache-hit share.

## Notes

Filed as one issue covering both scopes. Split into an epic with a child per
scope if scope 2 grows the push payload more than expected — scope 1 stands
alone and needs nothing from scope 2.
acceptance:
- `ccreport limits` prints a cache-hit column in all three tables, and
  `ccreport limits --json` carries the raw counts behind it.
- The ratio is defined in docs/calculation-reference.md.
- A window whose fill span has no records renders the absent marker rather than
  0%.
- The server ingests rate-limit snapshots from a push and stores them behind a
  numbered migration step.
- A dashboard page lists merged windows with the same columns, each row linking
  to that window's own page.
- pytest covers the new ratio, the new ingest path and the new routes;
  `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

title: Cache-hit share per rate-limit window, in the CLI table and on a server page
Merged spend on this machine: ccreport server pull and sync
description:
The status line's cost line totals this machine's records alone, so a person on two machines reads a 24H/7D/30D/AT number that is short by whatever the other machine spent. The server already holds both. Pull the merged totals back and render them, scoped to the account this machine is signed in to right now.

Decided in brainstorming:

1. Payload is aggregates, not records. One cost per pricing.ROLLING_WINDOWS name for the current account, plus as_of and each contributing machine's last push time. The key list stays derived from ROLLING_WINDOWS so tests/test_window_keys.py keeps covering it.

2. The account key is what accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now) resolves locally. The server widens it through db.accounts_with_alias, so a name typed on /settings/accounts selects what the email does.

3. Transport is the ingest response. /v1/report sits inside the network allowlist, so a pull through it returns nothing when the laptop is away from home, which is when the other machine's spend is most missing. Ingest is token-authed and outside that gate. Piggybacking costs no extra round trip and is already scoped to the pushing machine.

4. ccreport server pull posts a batch with no files and keeps only the totals from the reply. ccreport server sync is push then pull. Both spellings exist so each half is testable alone.

5. Rendering takes max(server_total, local_total) per window. The server total already holds this machine's pushed records but goes stale between pushes; excluding self and adding the local total instead would double count a call synced across two machines, which reports.load dedups server-side and the client cannot.

6. The project split stays local. A restricted machine pushes a null project, so *_project_cost cannot come back merged. The line becomes a merged machine-wide total over a local project cost.

7. Wiring mirrors push: a detached spawn on slow renders behind a pull_next_at meta key and push.attempt_interval(). The status line gains no import.

8. A staleness marker when the newest contributing push is older than an interval, so a machine that stopped pushing does not read as a machine that stopped spending.

Out of scope here: the S and W quota segments, which are native per-account already and need none of this. Later, once the table exists: ccu and forecast.py reading it.
acceptance: The status line's cost windows show the account's spend across every pushing machine, correct within one push interval, with the local project split intact and a marker when a contributor has gone quiet.

Cache-hit share per rate-limit window, in the CLI table and on a server page
description:
`ccreport limits` prints Peak, Samples, Fill, pp/h, Spend, $/pp, Extra and Hit
per window instance, and says nothing about how much of the work in that window
was served from the prompt cache. Cache-read tokens are the cheapest tokens on
the corpus, so a window with a high cache-hit share buys more work per rate-limit
point than one without, and $/pp alone cannot show why two windows differ.

The same history has no reader on the ccreport server: rate-limit snapshots are
a client-only table today, so the merged dashboard cannot show window history at
all.

## Scope 1 — CLI

Add a cache-hit column to the three `ccreport limits` tables (session, week,
scoped model) and the matching field to `ccreport limits --json`.

- `WindowSpend` (`src/ccreport/ccreport.py:2153`) carries `usd`, `per_pp`,
  `headroom_usd`, `extra_usd` and nothing token-shaped. The token counts are
  already on the records `_load_instance_spend` (`ccreport.py:2232`) loads:
  `TokenCounts.cache_read` and `.cache_create` in `src/ccreport/aggregate.py:36`.
- Measure it over the fill span (first sample to peak), the span `rise`,
  `burn_pph` and `usd` already share, so the row describes one stretch of time.
- Decide and document which ratio the column prints — cache_read over
  (input + cache_create + cache_read) is the reading that answers "how much of
  this window's context was already paid for". Put the definition in
  `docs/calculation-reference.md` section 9 beside the other window maths.
- `_limits_entry` (`ccreport.py:2335`) gains the raw numbers, not a formatted
  string, per its own docstring.
- A window with no priced records shows the absent marker, the same as Spend.

## Scope 2 — server page

Add a rate-limit window page to the server dashboard showing the same table,
merged across machines, with each window row linking to a page for that one
window instance.

- `rate_limit_snapshots` lives in cache.db alone (`src/ccreport/cache_db.py:329`).
  `push.py` sends `ccreport_records` only (`push.build_files`, `_records_for`,
  `push.py:415`), so this needs a new payload section, a server-side table and
  an ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`.
- Server schema changes go through `migrations.py`: a numbered `Step` appended
  to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in `src/ccreport/server/db.py`, per AGENTS.md.
- Snapshots carry no project and no session, so the restricted-machine
  redaction in `push.redact` has nothing to strip — confirm that reading before
  sending them, and decide whether a restricted machine sends them at all.
- The page belongs with the dashboard, not under `/settings`. Note that
  `/{dimension}/{key}` in `src/ccreport/server/pages.py:329` is the catch-all
  and matches whatever the named routes did not, so a new named route has to be
  registered before it.
- Charts follow the existing rules: fixed series order from
  `server/static/palette.js`, one scale per chart, vendored chart library, and
  assets linked through the `asset()` template global.
- The per-window detail page shows what the CLI's row summarizes plus the
  sample series that produced it: the fill curve over time, the records that
  filled it, and the cache-hit share.

## Notes

Filed as one issue covering both scopes. Split into an epic with a child per
scope if scope 2 grows the push payload more than expected — scope 1 stands
alone and needs nothing from scope 2.

- The server ingests rate-limit snapshots from a push and stores them behind a

title: Merged spend on this machine: ccreport server pull and sync
Push the extra-usage series so the merged window page can price Extra
description:
`ccreport limits` prints an Extra column: real dollars Anthropic billed as Extra
usage while a window ran, read from the `extra_usage_snapshots` table in
cache.db and joined by `ccreport._instance_extra` / `_ExtraIndex`
(src/ccreport/ccreport.py). The merged server page at `/limits` has no such
column, because nothing pushes that series — `push.build_files` sends records
and `push.build_samples` sends rate-limit samples, and neither touches
extra_usage_snapshots.

So a merged window shows Spend, $/pp and Cache but cannot say what the window
actually cost in credits. On this machine that figure is the only real money in
the report; everything else is an API-price valuation.

## What this needs

- A third payload section on the push, beside `files` and `samples`. The series
  is `(ts, spent)` — cumulative dollars within a billing month, written by slow
  status-line renders and pruned to 31 days by `cache_db.write_usage_cache`.
  Its own watermark, the way `cache_db.read_push_samples_at` works for samples.
- A server table behind a numbered `Step` appended to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in
  `src/ccreport/server/db.py` (the last is `Step(6, "rate_limit_samples")`),
  keyed on (machine_id, ts). The account has to travel with each reading, as it
  does for a sample: the client resolves it off `account_events`.
- An ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`, mirroring
  `db.store_rate_limit_samples`.
- The reader: `server/limits.py` currently passes `extra_usd=None` to
  `windows.instance_spend` with a comment saying the server has no such series.
  That comment and that argument are what this issue changes.

## Two things to decide before writing code

- **31 days of retention.** A machine that has not pushed in a month has lost
  the readings, so the server's copy is the only one — which makes it a
  database rather than a cache, unlike every other pushed table. Decide whether
  the server prunes it at all.
- **Is it per machine or per account?** The reading is cumulative spend on the
  billing account, so two machines signed into one account report the *same*
  dollars, not two halves of them. Summing them would double the figure.
  `windows` already merges samples on the account for this reason; the Extra
  series needs the same treatment, and probably a rule for which machine's
  readings win where both sampled the same window.

Acceptance criteria:
- A push carries the extra-usage series behind its own watermark, which
  `--full` and a policy change clear with the others.
- The server stores it behind a numbered migration step, and deleting a machine
  cascades it away.
- Two machines on one account do not double the figure.
- `/limits` and one window's page print Extra, with the absent marker where no
  reading bounds the span — never $0.00, which is a billed window that reads as
  a free one.
- pytest covers the push payload, the ingest path and the merged reading;
  `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

title: Push the extra-usage series so the merged window page can price Extra
Cache-hit share per rate-limit window, in the CLI table and on a server page
description:
`ccreport limits` prints Peak, Samples, Fill, pp/h, Spend, $/pp, Extra and Hit
per window instance, and says nothing about how much of the work in that window
was served from the prompt cache. Cache-read tokens are the cheapest tokens on
the corpus, so a window with a high cache-hit share buys more work per rate-limit
point than one without, and $/pp alone cannot show why two windows differ.

The same history has no reader on the ccreport server: rate-limit snapshots are
a client-only table today, so the merged dashboard cannot show window history at
all.

## Scope 1 — CLI

Add a cache-hit column to the three `ccreport limits` tables (session, week,
scoped model) and the matching field to `ccreport limits --json`.

- `WindowSpend` (`src/ccreport/ccreport.py:2153`) carries `usd`, `per_pp`,
  `headroom_usd`, `extra_usd` and nothing token-shaped. The token counts are
  already on the records `_load_instance_spend` (`ccreport.py:2232`) loads:
  `TokenCounts.cache_read` and `.cache_create` in `src/ccreport/aggregate.py:36`.
- Measure it over the fill span (first sample to peak), the span `rise`,

Merged spend on this machine: ccreport server pull and sync
description:
The status line's cost line totals this machine's records alone, so a person on two machines reads a 24H/7D/30D/AT number that is short by whatever the other machine spent. The server already holds both. Pull the other machines' totals back and add them, scoped to the account this machine is signed in to right now.

Decided in brainstorming:

1. Payload is aggregates, not records, at two grains. Per contributing machine: one cost per pricing.ROLLING_WINDOWS name for the status line, and one row per (machine, day, and where it is not redacted, project) for the CLI. Two grains because a rolling window is sub-day and cannot be derived from days, while a daily table cannot be derived from windows. The window key list stays derived from ROLLING_WINDOWS so tests/test_window_keys.py keeps covering it.

2. The account key is what accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now) resolves locally. The server widens it through db.accounts_with_alias, so a name typed on /settings/accounts selects what the email does.

3. Transport is the ingest response. /v1/report sits inside the network allowlist, so a pull through it returns nothing when the laptop is away from home, which is when the other machine's spend is most missing. Ingest is token-authed and outside that gate. Piggybacking costs no extra round trip and is already scoped to the pushing machine.

4. ccreport server pull posts a batch with no files and keeps only the totals from the reply. ccreport server sync is push then pull. Both spellings exist so each half is testable alone.

5. Nothing belonging to this machine comes back. The response excludes the requesting machine's own rows, so the local cache never holds a second, server-priced copy of records it already scanned — the server prices at ingest with its own pricing.py, and a pulled-back own total would put two prices on one call and let whichever the render reached win.

6. The exclusion is by dedup identity, not by machine id alone. The server drops its copy of the requesting machine's rows and then drops any remaining record whose dedup key this machine also pushed, so what it sends is the remainder that is genuinely elsewhere. Machine-id exclusion alone would double count a session log present on two machines: the server dedups across the set it folds, and a client adding its local total to that set's leftovers cannot see the overlap.

7. What arrives lands in its own tables and is never mixed into the local corpus: remote_window_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, window) and remote_day_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project), each holding the cost, that machine's last push time and this machine's fetched_at. Three reasons the marking is structural rather than a flag column: scan.py is the only writer of ccreport_files and ccreport_records and stays that way; a per-machine row is what makes a staleness marker per contributor possible; and every row in these tables is by construction another machine's, so nothing there can be misread as locally scanned. They reach an existing cache.db through a numbered Step appended to MIGRATION_CHAIN in cache_db.py, per the schema rule.

8. The status line renders local_total + sum(remote window rows) per window. Both halves are disjoint by construction, which is what 6 buys.

9. The project split stays local. A restricted machine pushes a null project, so *_project_cost cannot come back merged. The status line's cost window becomes a merged machine-wide total over a local project cost.

10. ccu does not read any of this. It is the live quota dashboard — what the API says about this account's windows right now — and a merged historic total is a different question on the same screen.

11. ccreport never opens a socket. It reads this machine's cache and nothing else, including under -A/--all, which merges the pulled remote tables — themselves local rows a detached pull wrote. A report is what a person types while looking at it and must not hang on a server that is down or out of reach, and a number that changes depending on whether the network was up is worse than one that is consistently this machine's. Only ccreport server pull, ccreport server sync, ccreport server push and the status line's detached spawn talk to the server; the explicitly typed ccreport --server URL stays what it is, a different command shape naming its host. Under -A the day, month and project tables merge; a session table cannot, because a restricted machine strips the session id, and -A says so rather than printing a short list as if it were whole.

12. Without -A, each table carries one note under it: what this account spent across every machine over the same range, how much of that is not on this machine, and that -A shows it. The number comes from the same remote tables, so the note cannot disagree with what -A then prints. No note where nothing was pulled, and no note for a table -A cannot merge.

13. Wiring mirrors push: a detached spawn on slow renders behind a pull_next_at meta key and push.attempt_interval(). The status line gains no import.

14. A staleness marker when the newest contributing push is older than an interval, so a machine that stopped pushing does not read as a machine that stopped spending. It shows in the status line and in the note.

15. The server memoizes the remainder per (account_uuid, requesting machine) against db.content_stamp, the key dashboard.cached_build already uses. A pull between pushes then costs a stamp read rather than a fold of this machine's whole dedup-key set against every other machine's records, which is what an empty-batch pull would otherwise run on a token-authed endpoint reachable from anywhere. No server-side rate limit: the stamp bounds the work, and pull_next_at bounds the calls from a client behaving as written.

16. remote_day_costs keeps every day, with no ageing and no fold to months. -A is then exact over all time, which is the whole point of the flag, and the alternative loses the month and project totals this epic exists to fix. The size cost is real and accepted: rows grow as machines times days times projects. What keeps it off the render path is that the status line reads remote_window_costs alone — remote_day_costs is opened by ccreport, which is typed, not rendered per frame. Revisit if a machine's table passes a size worth measuring.

17. Reads scope to accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now), not just writes, so a login switch cannot add a previous account's spend to this one's windows. The rows for that previous account stay: a switch back finds them without waiting for a pull, and a row nobody's read path selects costs storage alone. A stale row is therefore invisible rather than deleted, and the read-side filter is what makes that safe — it is not an optimisation and must not be dropped.

Out of scope here: the S and W quota segments, which are native per-account already and need none of this. Later: forecast.py reading the merged windows, and ccreport naming which machines a merged table covers.
acceptance: The status line's cost windows and ccreport -A show the account's spend across every pushing machine, correct within one push interval, with no record counted twice; a bare ccreport names the gap under each table; ccu is unchanged.

Normalize ccreport_records.file_path to an integer file id
description:
ccreport_records stores file_path as TEXT on every row, averaging 110 bytes across 11,230 distinct paths and 414,403 rows, then repeats it in idx_ccr_file_ts(file_path, ts). On one real machine that is 134 MB of table and 53 MB of index out of a 251 MB cache.db; a 'du -sm' of the parts and 'select name, sum(pgsize) from dbstat group by name' reproduce the split.

Replace it with an INTEGER id into ccreport_files. That table is WITHOUT ROWID and keyed on path, so it needs a rowid or an explicit id column of its own. Every reader in cache_db.py that selects or joins file_path changes with it: load_ccreport_records_under, _for_session, _for_paths, _since, _in_range, save_ccreport_files, and the ON DELETE CASCADE the records declare. scan.py is the only writer.

The change moves no number a report prints, so tests/golden/ must not move either.

Acceptance:
- A migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN converts the existing rows and rebuilds both indexes.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical before and after.
- cache.db on a corpus this size drops by roughly 90 MB after VACUUM.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Snapshot rotation leaves orphaned tmp files forever
description:
A machine had 2.1 GB of <date>.db.<pid>.tmp files in ~/.local/share/ccreport/snapshots, dated April through July, beside 682 MB of real snapshots. Each is a partial copy left by a process that died mid-backup under a naming scheme the current code no longer writes.

Nothing reaches them. _rotate_snapshots (cache_db.py:1022) globs _SNAPSHOT_GLOB and _SNAPSHOT_GLOB + .xz alone. _claim_snapshot_tmp (cache_db.py:1116) does clear a stale tmp, but only the fixed <date>.db.tmp the current writer picks, and only when a snapshot for that same date is being taken again.

Two parts:
- Sweep stale tmp files in _rotate_snapshots, matching <date>.db*.tmp and its -journal companion, under the same _SNAPSHOT_TMP_STALE_S the claim path uses, so a dead process cannot leave 200 MB behind for months.
- Keep the sweep off the live tmp: a concurrent writer holds one whose mtime is recent.

Acceptance:
- A pytest under tests/ writes an old <date>.db.<pid>.tmp plus a fresh <date>.db.tmp into a temp snapshot dir, runs rotation, and asserts the old one is gone and the fresh one stays.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Prune old ccreport_records behind authoritative rollups
description:
cache.db is 251 MB on one machine and ccreport_records is 207 MB of it. 352,388 of its 414,403 rows are older than 30 days. Deleting them today loses history, for two reasons.

First, 5,638 of the 11,230 files in ccreport_files no longer exist on disk. Claude Code rotated the logs; the rows are the only copy of what they held, which is why cache_db's sanity guard calls them irreplaceable and warns on a 10% drop.

Second, ccreport_rollups cannot stand in as it is. Its grain is (day, oslo_date, sid, project, model, account), so an hour, a cwd and a repo are already gone, and _rollup_fingerprint (ccreport.py:386) hashes pricing.py, the script hash, the account event log, the override rules and the local zone. title: Prune old ccreport_records behind authoritative rollups
Archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows
description:
cache.db is 214 MB after a VACUUM and ccreport_records is most of it: 414,403 rows, a 134 MB table, a 53 MB idx_ccr_file_ts and a 20 MB idx_ccr_sid. 352,388 of those rows are older than 30 days, and 5,638 of the 11,230 files in ccreport_files no longer exist on disk, so nothing will ever re-parse them.

Folded to (day, oslo_date, sid, project, model, cwd, repo, account) they are 3,329 rows. A 106:1 fold, which puts cache.db near 35 MB once ccreport-4q03 lands too.

The goal is no visible loss: nothing the server renders and nothing 'ccreport' prints may change.

## Why this is not the existing rollup table

ccreport_rollups is a cache, not a store. _rollup_fingerprint (ccreport.py:386) hashes pricing.py, the script hash, the account event log, the override rules and the local zone, and any mismatch rebuilds every row from records. Archived rows must be exempt from that rebuild and merged with freshly built ones, or the next price update leaves an empty history instead of a stale one.

## What must stay reachable

- The server is unaffected. It holds its own database and all 11,230 files here are pushed, so no page on it changes. What dies is 'push --full' as a way to rebuild a server from this machine; say so in the docs.
- The CLI renders nothing below a day. --since and --until take dates, --project, --account and --models sit inside the grain, and daily, monthly, projects, sessions and accounts all group at or above it.
- Identity goes in raw, the way ccreport_orphan_costs already stores it: project, cwd and repo unresolved, and the account boundary respected. Bake in a resolved name and a later 'ccreport merge' or 'ccreport adopt' cannot re-attribute an archived day. An archived row must also not straddle an account_events boundary, or adopt cannot split it.
- 'ccreport limits' is the one real conflict. It prices each window's fill span against the records covering it, over hours, and rate_limit_snapshots only ever grows. The cutoff has to stay behind the oldest snapshot that report still prices, not at a fixed 30 days.

## Speed

Warm 'ccreport' is 0.91 s; a cold run that rebuilt rollups was 4.96 s. Archived rows never rebuild, so that worst case goes with them.

Acceptance:
- An archive table plus a migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN.
- Archived rows are exempt from the rollup fingerprint rebuild and merge with live ones.
- 'ccreport archive --dry-run' prints what it would fold and what it would drop.
- The cutoff is derived against min(ts) in rate_limit_snapshots, not hardcoded.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical across an archive run.
- A test asserts merge, unmerge and adopt still re-attribute an archived span.
- The sanity guard in cache_db does not fire on an archive run.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Point 16 of that epic keeps remote_day_costs at (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project) with no ageing and no fold to months, accepts the growth, and says to revisit when a machine's table passes a size worth measuring.
