title: Archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows
Merged spend on this machine: ccreport server pull and sync
description:
The status line's cost line totals this machine's records alone, so a person on two machines reads a 24H/7D/30D/AT number that is short by whatever the other machine spent. The server already holds both. Pull the other machines' totals back and add them, scoped to the account this machine is signed in to right now.

Decided in brainstorming:

1. Payload is aggregates, not records, at two grains. Per contributing machine: one cost per pricing.ROLLING_WINDOWS name for the status line, and one row per (machine, day, and where it is not redacted, project) for the CLI. Two grains because a rolling window is sub-day and cannot be derived from days, while a daily table cannot be derived from windows. The window key list stays derived from ROLLING_WINDOWS so tests/test_window_keys.py keeps covering it.

2. The account key is what accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now) resolves locally. The server widens it through db.accounts_with_alias, so a name typed on /settings/accounts selects what the email does.

3. Transport is the ingest response. /v1/report sits inside the network allowlist, so a pull through it returns nothing when the laptop is away from home, which is when the other machine's spend is most missing. Ingest is token-authed and outside that gate. Piggybacking costs no extra round trip and is already scoped to the pushing machine.

4. ccreport server pull posts a batch with no files and keeps only the totals from the reply. ccreport server sync is push then pull. Both spellings exist so each half is testable alone.

5. Nothing belonging to this machine comes back. The response excludes the requesting machine's own rows, so the local cache never holds a second, server-priced copy of records it already scanned — the server prices at ingest with its own pricing.py, and a pulled-back own total would put two prices on one call and let whichever the render reached win.

6. The exclusion is by dedup identity, not by machine id alone. The server drops its copy of the requesting machine's rows and then drops any remaining record whose dedup key this machine also pushed, so what it sends is the remainder that is genuinely elsewhere. Machine-id exclusion alone would double count a session log present on two machines: the server dedups across the set it folds, and a client adding its local total to that set's leftovers cannot see the overlap.

7. What arrives lands in its own tables and is never mixed into the local corpus: remote_window_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, window) and remote_day_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project), each holding the cost, that machine's last push time and this machine's fetched_at. Three reasons the marking is structural rather than a flag column: scan.py is the only writer of ccreport_files and ccreport_records and stays that way; a per-machine row is what makes a staleness marker per contributor possible; and every row in these tables is by construction another machine's, so nothing there can be misread as locally scanned. They reach an existing cache.db through a numbered Step appended to MIGRATION_CHAIN in cache_db.py, per the schema rule.

8. The status line renders local_total + sum(remote window rows) per window. Both halves are disjoint by construction, which is what 6 buys.

9. The project split stays local. A restricted machine pushes a null project, so *_project_cost cannot come back merged. The status line's cost window becomes a merged machine-wide total over a local project cost.

10. ccu does not read any of this. It is the live quota dashboard — what the API says about this account's windows right now — and a merged historic total is a different question on the same screen.

11. ccreport never opens a socket. It reads this machine's cache and nothing else, including under -A/--all, which merges the pulled remote tables — themselves local rows a detached pull wrote. A report is what a person types while looking at it and must not hang on a server that is down or out of reach, and a number that changes depending on whether the network was up is worse than one that is consistently this machine's. Only ccreport server pull, ccreport server sync, ccreport server push and the status line's detached spawn talk to the server; the explicitly typed ccreport --server URL stays what it is, a different command shape naming its host. Under -A the day, month and project tables merge; a session table cannot, because a restricted machine strips the session id, and -A says so rather than printing a short list as if it were whole.

12. Without -A, each table carries one note under it: what this account spent across every machine over the same range, how much of that is not on this machine, and that -A shows it. The number comes from the same remote tables, so the note cannot disagree with what -A then prints. No note where nothing was pulled, and no note for a table -A cannot merge.

13. Wiring mirrors push: a detached spawn on slow renders behind a pull_next_at meta key and push.attempt_interval(). The status line gains no import.

14. A staleness marker when the newest contributing push is older than an interval, so a machine that stopped pushing does not read as a machine that stopped spending. It shows in the status line and in the note.

15. The server memoizes the remainder per (account_uuid, requesting machine) against db.content_stamp, the key dashboard.cached_build already uses. A pull between pushes then costs a stamp read rather than a fold of this machine's whole dedup-key set against every other machine's records, which is what an empty-batch pull would otherwise run on a token-authed endpoint reachable from anywhere. No server-side rate limit: the stamp bounds the work, and pull_next_at bounds the calls from a client behaving as written.

16. remote_day_costs keeps every day, with no ageing and no fold to months. -A is then exact over all time, which is the whole point of the flag, and the alternative loses the month and project totals this epic exists to fix. The size cost is real and accepted: rows grow as machines times days times projects. What keeps it off the render path is that the status line reads remote_window_costs alone — remote_day_costs is opened by ccreport, which is typed, not rendered per frame. Revisit if a machine's table passes a size worth measuring.

17. Reads scope to accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now), not just writes, so a login switch cannot add a previous account's spend to this one's windows. The rows for that previous account stay: a switch back finds them without waiting for a pull, and a row nobody's read path selects costs storage alone. A stale row is therefore invisible rather than deleted, and the read-side filter is what makes that safe — it is not an optimisation and must not be dropped.

Out of scope here: the S and W quota segments, which are native per-account already and need none of this. Later: forecast.py reading the merged windows, and ccreport naming which machines a merged table covers.
acceptance: The status line's cost windows and ccreport -A show the account's spend across every pushing machine, correct within one push interval, with no record counted twice; a bare ccreport names the gap under each table; ccu is unchanged.

title: Merged spend on this machine: ccreport server pull and sync
Push the extra-usage series so the merged window page can price Extra
description:
`ccreport limits` prints an Extra column: real dollars Anthropic billed as Extra
usage while a window ran, read from the `extra_usage_snapshots` table in
cache.db and joined by `ccreport._instance_extra` / `_ExtraIndex`
(src/ccreport/ccreport.py). The merged server page at `/limits` has no such
column, because nothing pushes that series — `push.build_files` sends records
and `push.build_samples` sends rate-limit samples, and neither touches
extra_usage_snapshots.

So a merged window shows Spend, $/pp and Cache but cannot say what the window
actually cost in credits. On this machine that figure is the only real money in
the report; everything else is an API-price valuation.

## What this needs

- A third payload section on the push, beside `files` and `samples`. The series
  is `(ts, spent)` — cumulative dollars within a billing month, written by slow
  status-line renders and pruned to 31 days by `cache_db.write_usage_cache`.
  Its own watermark, the way `cache_db.read_push_samples_at` works for samples.
- A server table behind a numbered `Step` appended to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in
  `src/ccreport/server/db.py` (the last is `Step(6, "rate_limit_samples")`),
  keyed on (machine_id, ts). The account has to travel with each reading, as it
  does for a sample: the client resolves it off `account_events`.
- An ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`, mirroring
  `db.store_rate_limit_samples`.
- The reader: `server/limits.py` currently passes `extra_usd=None` to
  `windows.instance_spend` with a comment saying the server has no such series.
  That comment and that argument are what this issue changes.

## Two things to decide before writing code

- **31 days of retention.** A machine that has not pushed in a month has lost
  the readings, so the server's copy is the only one — which makes it a
  database rather than a cache, unlike every other pushed table. Decide whether
  the server prunes it at all.
- **Is it per machine or per account?** The reading is cumulative spend on the
  billing account, so two machines signed into one account report the *same*
  dollars, not two halves of them. Summing them would double the figure.
  `windows` already merges samples on the account for this reason; the Extra
  series needs the same treatment, and probably a rule for which machine's
  readings win where both sampled the same window.

Acceptance criteria:
- A push carries the extra-usage series behind its own watermark, which
  `--full` and a policy change clear with the others.
- The server stores it behind a numbered migration step, and deleting a machine
  cascades it away.
- Two machines on one account do not double the figure.
- `/limits` and one window's page print Extra, with the absent marker where no
  reading bounds the span — never $0.00, which is a billed window that reads as
  a free one.
- pytest covers the push payload, the ingest path and the merged reading;
  `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
notes:
Related: ccreport-3soc (archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows). No dependency edge either way.

The retention question under 'Two things to decide' - whether the server prunes the extra-usage series, given a machine that has not pushed in a month has lost it - is the same authority question ccreport-3soc answers on the client: when the source is gone, which copy is the database. Settle both the same way rather than one per issue.

Two measurements from this machine, taken 2026-08-19:

- extra_usage_snapshots holds 0 rows here. There is no local series to push right now, so the push payload and the ingest path need a fixture rather than a live corpus to test against.
- cache_db.py:1728 deletes rows older than 31 days on every usage-cache write. So 'ccreport limits' already cannot print Extra beyond 31 days on any machine, whatever the server does. Worth stating on the merged /limits page too: an absent Extra past 31 days is retention, not a free window.

Snapshot rotation leaves orphaned tmp files forever
description:
A machine had 2.1 GB of <date>.db.<pid>.tmp files in ~/.local/share/ccreport/snapshots, dated April through July, beside 682 MB of real snapshots. Each is a partial copy left by a process that died mid-backup under a naming scheme the current code no longer writes.

Nothing reaches them. _rotate_snapshots (cache_db.py:1022) globs _SNAPSHOT_GLOB and _SNAPSHOT_GLOB + .xz alone. _claim_snapshot_tmp (cache_db.py:1116) does clear a stale tmp, but only the fixed <date>.db.tmp the current writer picks, and only when a snapshot for that same date is being taken again.

Two parts:
- Sweep stale tmp files in _rotate_snapshots, matching <date>.db*.tmp and its -journal companion, under the same _SNAPSHOT_TMP_STALE_S the claim path uses, so a dead process cannot leave 200 MB behind for months.
- Keep the sweep off the live tmp: a concurrent writer holds one whose mtime is recent.

Acceptance:
- A pytest under tests/ writes an old <date>.db.<pid>.tmp plus a fresh <date>.db.tmp into a temp snapshot dir, runs rotation, and asserts the old one is gone and the fresh one stays.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Normalize ccreport_records.file_path to an integer file id
description:
ccreport_records stores file_path as TEXT on every row, averaging 110 bytes across 11,230 distinct paths and 414,403 rows, then repeats it in idx_ccr_file_ts(file_path, ts). On one real machine that is 134 MB of table and 53 MB of index out of a 251 MB cache.db; a 'du -sm' of the parts and 'select name, sum(pgsize) from dbstat group by name' reproduce the split.

Replace it with an INTEGER id into ccreport_files. That table is WITHOUT ROWID and keyed on path, so it needs a rowid or an explicit id column of its own. Every reader in cache_db.py that selects or joins file_path changes with it: load_ccreport_records_under, _for_session, _for_paths, _since, _in_range, save_ccreport_files, and the ON DELETE CASCADE the records declare. scan.py is the only writer.

The change moves no number a report prints, so tests/golden/ must not move either.

Acceptance:
- A migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN converts the existing rows and rebuilds both indexes.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical before and after.
- cache.db on a corpus this size drops by roughly 90 MB after VACUUM.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows
description:
cache.db is 214 MB after a VACUUM and ccreport_records is most of it: 414,403 rows, a 134 MB table, a 53 MB idx_ccr_file_ts and a 20 MB idx_ccr_sid. 352,388 of those rows are older than 30 days, and 5,638 of the 11,230 files in ccreport_files no longer exist on disk, so nothing will ever re-parse them.

Folded to (day, oslo_date, sid, project, model, cwd, repo, account) they are 3,329 rows. A 106:1 fold, which puts cache.db near 35 MB once ccreport-4q03 lands too.

The goal is no visible loss: nothing the server renders and nothing 'ccreport' prints may change.

## Why this is not the existing rollup table

ccreport_rollups is a cache, not a store. _rollup_fingerprint (ccreport.py:386) hashes pricing.py, the script hash, the account event log, the override rules and the local zone, and any mismatch rebuilds every row from records. Archived rows must be exempt from that rebuild and merged with freshly built ones, or the next price update leaves an empty history instead of a stale one.

## What must stay reachable

- The server is unaffected. It holds its own database and all 11,230 files here are pushed, so no page on it changes. What dies is 'push --full' as a way to rebuild a server from this machine; say so in the docs.
- The CLI renders nothing below a day. --since and --until take dates, --project, --account and --models sit inside the grain, and daily, monthly, projects, sessions and accounts all group at or above it.
- Identity goes in raw, the way ccreport_orphan_costs already stores it: project, cwd and repo unresolved, and the account boundary respected. Bake in a resolved name and a later 'ccreport merge' or 'ccreport adopt' cannot re-attribute an archived day. An archived row must also not straddle an account_events boundary, or adopt cannot split it.
- 'ccreport limits' is the one real conflict. It prices each window's fill span against the records covering it, over hours, and rate_limit_snapshots only ever grows. The cutoff has to stay behind the oldest snapshot that report still prices, not at a fixed 30 days.

## Speed

Warm 'ccreport' is 0.91 s; a cold run that rebuilt rollups was 4.96 s. Archived rows never rebuild, so that worst case goes with them.

Acceptance:
- An archive table plus a migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN.
- Archived rows are exempt from the rollup fingerprint rebuild and merge with live ones.
- 'ccreport archive --dry-run' prints what it would fold and what it would drop.
- The cutoff is derived against min(ts) in rate_limit_snapshots, not hardcoded.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical across an archive run.
- A test asserts merge, unmerge and adopt still re-attribute an archived span.
- The sanity guard in cache_db does not fire on an archive run.
- just lint-all and just test pass.
notes:
Related: ccreport-4x0s and ccreport-3l3z. Neither blocks this and this blocks neither, so no dependency edge is wired.

## ccreport-4x0s (pull and sync)

Point 16 of that epic keeps remote_day_costs at (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project) with no ageing and no fold to months, accepts the growth, and says to revisit when a machine's table passes a size worth measuring. This is that revisit, and the fold measured here is 106:1 on 352,388 rows.

Build the archive at a grain that agrees with remote_day_costs, so 'ccreport -A' folds an archived local day and a pulled remote day through one path. The archive carries sid, cwd and repo on top, which a pushed remote row does not; that is fine as long as the day, project and account columns line up.

Both add tables to MIGRATION_CHAIN in cache_db.py, so whichever lands second takes the next step number. Do not reserve one in advance.

Non-conflict, worth not rediscovering: point 6 has the server compute the pull remainder from the dedup keys this machine already pushed, using its own copy. An archive that drops the dk column locally therefore does not break the exclusion.

## ccreport-3l3z (push the extra-usage series)

Its open question - does the server prune that series at all, or is its copy the only one - is the same authority question this issue answers locally. Whatever is decided there about a series whose source is gone should read the same way here.

It also narrows the cutoff constraint above. cache_db.py:1728 already deletes extra_usage_snapshots older than 31 days, so 'ccreport limits' cannot price the Extra column beyond 31 days on any machine today. Only rate_limit_snapshots, which never ages out, constrains where the archive cutoff can sit.

Push the extra-usage series so the merged window page can price Extra
description:
`ccreport limits` prints an Extra column: real dollars Anthropic billed as Extra
usage while a window ran, read from the `extra_usage_snapshots` table in
cache.db and joined by `ccreport._instance_extra` / `_ExtraIndex`
(src/ccreport/ccreport.py). The merged server page at `/limits` has no such
column, because nothing pushes that series — `push.build_files` sends records
and `push.build_samples` sends rate-limit samples, and neither touches
extra_usage_snapshots.

So a merged window shows Spend, $/pp and Cache but cannot say what the window
actually cost in credits. On this machine that figure is the only real money in
the report; everything else is an API-price valuation.

## What this needs

- A third payload section on the push, beside `files` and `samples`. The series
  is `(ts, spent)` — cumulative dollars within a billing month, written by slow
  status-line renders and pruned to 31 days by `cache_db.write_usage_cache`.
  Its own watermark, the way `cache_db.read_push_samples_at` works for samples.
- A server table behind a numbered `Step` appended to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in
  `src/ccreport/server/db.py` (the last is `Step(6, "rate_limit_samples")`),
  keyed on (machine_id, ts). The account has to travel with each reading, as it
  does for a sample: the client resolves it off `account_events`.
- An ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`, mirroring
  `db.store_rate_limit_samples`.
- The reader: `server/limits.py` currently passes `extra_usd=None` to
  `windows.instance_spend` with a comment saying the server has no such series.
  That comment and that argument are what this issue changes.

## Two things to decide before writing code

- **31 days of retention.** A machine that has not pushed in a month has lost
  the readings, so the server's copy is the only one — which makes it a
  database rather than a cache, unlike every other pushed table. Decide whether
  the server prunes it at all.
- **Is it per machine or per account?** The reading is cumulative spend on the
  billing account, so two machines signed into one account report the *same*
  dollars, not two halves of them. Summing them would double the figure.
  `windows` already merges samples on the account for this reason; the Extra
  series needs the same treatment, and probably a rule for which machine's
  readings win where both sampled the same window.

Acceptance criteria:
- A push carries the extra-usage series behind its own watermark, which
  `--full` and a policy change clear with the others.
- The server stores it behind a numbered migration step, and deleting a machine
  cascades it away.
- Two machines on one account do not double the figure.
- `/limits` and one window's page print Extra, with the absent marker where no
  reading bounds the span — never $0.00, which is a billed window that reads as
  a free one.
- pytest covers the push payload, the ingest path and the merged reading;
  `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

Decided in brainstorming:

1. Payload is aggregates, not records, at two grains. Per contributing machine: one cost per pricing.ROLLING_WINDOWS name for the status line, and one row per (machine, day, and where it is not redacted, project) for the CLI. Two grains because a rolling window is sub-day and cannot be derived from days, while a daily table cannot be derived from windows. The window key list stays derived from ROLLING_WINDOWS so tests/test_window_keys.py keeps covering it.

2. The account key is what accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now) resolves locally. The server widens it through db.accounts_with_alias, so a name typed on /settings/accounts selects what the email does.

3. Transport is the ingest response. /v1/report sits inside the network allowlist, so a pull through it returns nothing when the laptop is away from home, which is when the other machine's spend is most missing. Ingest is token-authed and outside that gate. Piggybacking costs no extra round trip and is already scoped to the pushing machine.

4. ccreport server pull posts a batch with no files and keeps only the totals from the reply. ccreport server sync is push then pull. Both spellings exist so each half is testable alone.

5. Nothing belonging to this machine comes back. The response excludes the requesting machine's own rows, so the local cache never holds a second, server-priced copy of records it already scanned — the server prices at ingest with its own pricing.py, and a pulled-back own total would put two prices on one call and let whichever the render reached win.

6. The exclusion is by dedup identity, not by machine id alone. The server drops its copy of the requesting machine's rows and then drops any remaining record whose dedup key this machine also pushed, so what it sends is the remainder that is genuinely elsewhere. Machine-id exclusion alone would double count a session log present on two machines: the server dedups across the set it folds, and a client adding its local total to that set's leftovers cannot see the overlap.

7. What arrives lands in its own tables and is never mixed into the local corpus: remote_window_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, window) and remote_day_costs keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project), each holding the cost, that machine's last push time and this machine's fetched_at. Three reasons the marking is structural rather than a flag column: scan.py is the only writer of ccreport_files and ccreport_records and stays that way; a per-machine row is what makes a staleness marker per contributor possible; and every row in these tables is by construction another machine's, so nothing there can be misread as locally scanned. They reach an existing cache.db through a numbered Step appended to MIGRATION_CHAIN in cache_db.py, per the schema rule.

8. The status line renders local_total + sum(remote window rows) per window. Both halves are disjoint by construction, which is what 6 buys.

9. The project split stays local. A restricted machine pushes a null project, so *_project_cost cannot come back merged. The status line's cost window becomes a merged machine-wide total over a local project cost.

10. ccu does not read any of this. It is the live quota dashboard — what the API says about this account's windows right now — and a merged historic total is a different question on the same screen.

11. ccreport never opens a socket. It reads this machine's cache and nothing else, including under -A/--all, which merges the pulled remote tables — themselves local rows a detached pull wrote. A report is what a person types while looking at it and must not hang on a server that is down or out of reach, and a number that changes depending on whether the network was up is worse than one that is consistently this machine's. Only ccreport server pull, ccreport server sync, ccreport server push and the status line's detached spawn talk to the server; the explicitly typed ccreport --server URL stays what it is, a different command shape naming its host. Under -A the day, month and project tables merge; a session table cannot, because a restricted machine strips the session id, and -A says so rather than printing a short list as if it were whole.

12. Without -A, each table carries one note under it: what this account spent across every machine over the same range, how much of that is not on this machine, and that -A shows it. The number comes from the same remote tables, so the note cannot disagree with what -A then prints. No note where nothing was pulled, and no note for a table -A cannot merge.

13. Wiring mirrors push: a detached spawn on slow renders behind a pull_next_at meta key and push.attempt_interval(). The status line gains no import.

14. A staleness marker when the newest contributing push is older than an interval, so a machine that stopped pushing does not read as a machine that stopped spending. It shows in the status line and in the note.

15. The server memoizes the remainder per (account_uuid, requesting machine) against db.content_stamp, the key dashboard.cached_build already uses. A pull between pushes then costs a stamp read rather than a fold of this machine's whole dedup-key set against every other machine's records, which is what an empty-batch pull would otherwise run on a token-authed endpoint reachable from anywhere. No server-side rate limit: the stamp bounds the work, and pull_next_at bounds the calls from a client behaving as written.

16. remote_day_costs keeps every day, with no ageing and no fold to months. -A is then exact over all time, which is the whole point of the flag, and the alternative loses the month and project totals this epic exists to fix. The size cost is real and accepted: rows grow as machines times days times projects. What keeps it off the render path is that the status line reads remote_window_costs alone — remote_day_costs is opened by ccreport, which is typed, not rendered per frame. Revisit if a machine's table passes a size worth measuring.

17. Reads scope to accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now), not just writes, so a login switch cannot add a previous account's spend to this one's windows. The rows for that previous account stay: a switch back finds them without waiting for a pull, and a row nobody's read path selects costs storage alone. A stale row is therefore invisible rather than deleted, and the read-side filter is what makes that safe — it is not an optimisation and must not be dropped.

Out of scope here: the S and W quota segments, which are native per-account already and need none of this. Later: forecast.py reading the merged windows, and ccreport naming which machines a merged table covers.
acceptance: The status line's cost windows and ccreport -A show the account's spend across every pushing machine, correct within one push interval, with no record counted twice; a bare ccreport names the gap under each table; ccu is unchanged.

Related: ccreport-3soc (archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows). No dependency edge either way; neither blocks the other.

Snapshot rotation leaves orphaned tmp files forever
description:
A machine had 2.1 GB of <date>.db.<pid>.tmp files in ~/.local/share/ccreport/snapshots, dated April through July, beside 682 MB of real snapshots. Each is a partial copy left by a process that died mid-backup under a naming scheme the current code no longer writes.

Nothing reaches them. _rotate_snapshots (cache_db.py:1022) globs _SNAPSHOT_GLOB and _SNAPSHOT_GLOB + .xz alone. _claim_snapshot_tmp (cache_db.py:1116) does clear a stale tmp, but only the fixed <date>.db.tmp the current writer picks, and only when a snapshot for that same date is being taken again.

Two parts:
- Sweep stale tmp files in _rotate_snapshots, matching <date>.db*.tmp and its -journal companion, under the same _SNAPSHOT_TMP_STALE_S the claim path uses, so a dead process cannot leave 200 MB behind for months.
- Keep the sweep off the live tmp: a concurrent writer holds one whose mtime is recent.

Acceptance:
- A pytest under tests/ writes an old <date>.db.<pid>.tmp plus a fresh <date>.db.tmp into a temp snapshot dir, runs rotation, and asserts the old one is gone and the fresh one stays.
- just lint-all and just test pass.
closed_reason: Stale snapshot tmp files are swept on rotation

Normalize ccreport_records.file_path to an integer file id
description:
ccreport_records stores file_path as TEXT on every row, averaging 110 bytes across 11,230 distinct paths and 414,403 rows, then repeats it in idx_ccr_file_ts(file_path, ts). On one real machine that is 134 MB of table and 53 MB of index out of a 251 MB cache.db; a 'du -sm' of the parts and 'select name, sum(pgsize) from dbstat group by name' reproduce the split.

Replace it with an INTEGER id into ccreport_files. That table is WITHOUT ROWID and keyed on path, so it needs a rowid or an explicit id column of its own. Every reader in cache_db.py that selects or joins file_path changes with it: load_ccreport_records_under, _for_session, _for_paths, _since, _in_range, save_ccreport_files, and the ON DELETE CASCADE the records declare. scan.py is the only writer.

The change moves no number a report prints, so tests/golden/ must not move either.

Acceptance:
- A migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN converts the existing rows and rebuilds both indexes.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical before and after.
- cache.db on a corpus this size drops by roughly 90 MB after VACUUM.
- just lint-all and just test pass.
closed_reason: file_path is an integer file_id; cache.db 214 -> 126 MB

Archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows
description:
cache.db is 214 MB after a VACUUM and ccreport_records is most of it: 414,403 rows, a 134 MB table, a 53 MB idx_ccr_file_ts and a 20 MB idx_ccr_sid. 352,388 of those rows are older than 30 days, and 5,638 of the 11,230 files in ccreport_files no longer exist on disk, so nothing will ever re-parse them.

Folded to (day, oslo_date, sid, project, model, cwd, repo, account) they are 3,329 rows. A 106:1 fold, which puts cache.db near 35 MB once ccreport-4q03 lands too.

The goal is no visible loss: nothing the server renders and nothing 'ccreport' prints may change.

## Why this is not the existing rollup table

ccreport_rollups is a cache, not a store. _rollup_fingerprint (ccreport.py:386) hashes pricing.py, the script hash, the account event log, the override rules and the local zone, and any mismatch rebuilds every row from records. Archived rows must be exempt from that rebuild and merged with freshly built ones, or the next price update leaves an empty history instead of a stale one.

## What must stay reachable

- The server is unaffected. It holds its own database and all 11,230 files here are pushed, so no page on it changes. What dies is 'push --full' as a way to rebuild a server from this machine; say so in the docs.
- The CLI renders nothing below a day. --since and --until take dates, --project, --account and --models sit inside the grain, and daily, monthly, projects, sessions and accounts all group at or above it.
- Identity goes in raw, the way ccreport_orphan_costs already stores it: project, cwd and repo unresolved, and the account boundary respected. Bake in a resolved name and a later 'ccreport merge' or 'ccreport adopt' cannot re-attribute an archived day. An archived row must also not straddle an account_events boundary, or adopt cannot split it.
- 'ccreport limits' is the one real conflict. It prices each window's fill span against the records covering it, over hours, and rate_limit_snapshots only ever grows. The cutoff has to stay behind the oldest snapshot that report still prices, not at a fixed 30 days.

## Speed

Warm 'ccreport' is 0.91 s; a cold run that rebuilt rollups was 4.96 s. Archived rows never rebuild, so that worst case goes with them.

Acceptance:
- An archive table plus a migration Step in cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN.
- Archived rows are exempt from the rollup fingerprint rebuild and merge with live ones.
- 'ccreport archive --dry-run' prints what it would fold and what it would drop.
- The cutoff is derived against min(ts) in rate_limit_snapshots, not hardcoded.
- tests/golden/ is byte-identical across an archive run.
- A test asserts merge, unmerge and adopt still re-attribute an archived span.
- The sanity guard in cache_db does not fire on an archive run.
- just lint-all and just test pass.
notes:
Related: ccreport-4x0s and ccreport-3l3z. Neither blocks this and this blocks neither, so no dependency edge is wired.

## ccreport-4x0s (pull and sync)

Point 16 of that epic keeps remote_day_costs at (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project) with no ageing and no fold to months, accepts the growth, and says to revisit when a machine's table passes a size worth measuring. This is that revisit, and the fold measured here is 106:1 on 352,388 rows.

Build the archive at a grain that agrees with remote_day_costs, so 'ccreport -A' folds an archived local day and a pulled remote day through one path. The archive carries sid, cwd and repo on top, which a pushed remote row does not; that is fine as long as the day, project and account columns line up.

Both add tables to MIGRATION_CHAIN in cache_db.py, so whichever lands second takes the next step number. Do not reserve one in advance.

Non-conflict, worth not rediscovering: point 6 has the server compute the pull remainder from the dedup keys this machine already pushed, using its own copy. An archive that drops the dk column locally therefore does not break the exclusion.

## ccreport-3l3z (push the extra-usage series)

Its open question - does the server prune that series at all, or is its copy the only one - is the same authority question this issue answers locally. Whatever is decided there about a series whose source is gone should read the same way here.

It also narrows the cutoff constraint above. cache_db.py:1728 already deletes extra_usage_snapshots older than 31 days, so 'ccreport limits' cannot price the Extra column beyond 31 days on any machine today. Only rate_limit_snapshots, which never ages out, constrains where the archive cutoff can sit.
closed_reason: ccreport archive folds purged files to day rows; run on this machine, reports unchanged

title: Archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows
Push the extra-usage series so the merged window page can price Extra
description:
`ccreport limits` prints an Extra column: real dollars Anthropic billed as Extra
usage while a window ran, read from the `extra_usage_snapshots` table in
cache.db and joined by `ccreport._instance_extra` / `_ExtraIndex`
(src/ccreport/ccreport.py). The merged server page at `/limits` has no such
column, because nothing pushes that series — `push.build_files` sends records
and `push.build_samples` sends rate-limit samples, and neither touches
extra_usage_snapshots.

So a merged window shows Spend, $/pp and Cache but cannot say what the window
actually cost in credits. On this machine that figure is the only real money in
the report; everything else is an API-price valuation.

## What this needs

- A third payload section on the push, beside `files` and `samples`. The series
  is `(ts, spent)` — cumulative dollars within a billing month, written by slow
  status-line renders and pruned to 31 days by `cache_db.write_usage_cache`.
  Its own watermark, the way `cache_db.read_push_samples_at` works for samples.
- A server table behind a numbered `Step` appended to `MIGRATION_CHAIN` in
  `src/ccreport/server/db.py` (the last is `Step(6, "rate_limit_samples")`),
  keyed on (machine_id, ts). The account has to travel with each reading, as it
  does for a sample: the client resolves it off `account_events`.
- An ingest path in `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py`, mirroring
  `db.store_rate_limit_samples`.
- The reader: `server/limits.py` currently passes `extra_usd=None` to
  `windows.instance_spend` with a comment saying the server has no such series.
  That comment and that argument are what this issue changes.

## Two things to decide before writing code

- **31 days of retention.** A machine that has not pushed in a month has lost
  the readings, so the server's copy is the only one — which makes it a
  database rather than a cache, unlike every other pushed table. Decide whether
  the server prunes it at all.
- **Is it per machine or per account?** The reading is cumulative spend on the
  billing account, so two machines signed into one account report the *same*
  dollars, not two halves of them. Summing them would double the figure.
  `windows` already merges samples on the account for this reason; the Extra
  series needs the same treatment, and probably a rule for which machine's
  readings win where both sampled the same window.

Acceptance criteria:
- A push carries the extra-usage series behind its own watermark, which
  `--full` and a policy change clear with the others.
- The server stores it behind a numbered migration step, and deleting a machine
  cascades it away.
- Two machines on one account do not double the figure.
- `/limits` and one window's page print Extra, with the absent marker where no
  reading bounds the span — never $0.00, which is a billed window that reads as
  a free one.
- pytest covers the push payload, the ingest path and the merged reading;
  `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
notes:
Related: ccreport-3soc (archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows). No dependency edge either way.

The retention question under 'Two things to decide' - whether the server prunes the extra-usage series, given a machine that has not pushed in a month has lost it - is the same authority question ccreport-3soc answers on the client: when the source is gone, which copy is the database. Settle both the same way rather than one per issue.

Two measurements from this machine, taken 2026-08-19:

- extra_usage_snapshots holds 0 rows here. There is no local series to push right now, so the push payload and the ingest path need a fixture rather than a live corpus to test against.
- cache_db.py:1728 deletes rows older than 31 days on every usage-cache write. So 'ccreport limits' already cannot print Extra beyond 31 days on any machine, whatever the server does. Worth stating on the merged /limits page too: an absent Extra past 31 days is retention, not a free window.
closed_reason: Extra-usage series pushes behind its own watermark; /limits prices Extra

10. ccu does not read any of this. It is the live quota dashboard — what the API says about this account's windows right now — and a merged historic total is a different question on the same screen.

11. ccreport never opens a socket. It reads this machine's cache and nothing else, including under -A/--all, which merges the pulled remote tables — themselves local rows a detached pull wrote. A report is what a person types while looking at it and must not hang on a server that is down or out of reach, and a number that changes depending on whether the network was up is worse than one that is consistently this machine's. Only ccreport server pull, ccreport server sync, ccreport server push and the status line's detached spawn talk to the server; the explicitly typed ccreport --server URL stays what it is, a different command shape naming its host. Under -A the day, month and project tables merge; a session table cannot, because a restricted machine strips the session id, and -A says so rather than printing a short list as if it were whole.

12. Without -A, each table carries one note under it: what this account spent across every machine over the same range, how much of that is not on this machine, and that -A shows it. The number comes from the same remote tables, so the note cannot disagree with what -A then prints. No note where nothing was pulled, and no note for a table -A cannot merge.

13. Wiring mirrors push: a detached spawn on slow renders behind a pull_next_at meta key and push.attempt_interval(). The status line gains no import.

14. A staleness marker when the newest contributing push is older than an interval, so a machine that stopped pushing does not read as a machine that stopped spending. It shows in the status line and in the note.

15. The server memoizes the remainder per (account_uuid, requesting machine) against db.content_stamp, the key dashboard.cached_build already uses. A pull between pushes then costs a stamp read rather than a fold of this machine's whole dedup-key set against every other machine's records, which is what an empty-batch pull would otherwise run on a token-authed endpoint reachable from anywhere. No server-side rate limit: the stamp bounds the work, and pull_next_at bounds the calls from a client behaving as written.

16. remote_day_costs keeps every day, with no ageing and no fold to months. -A is then exact over all time, which is the whole point of the flag, and the alternative loses the month and project totals this epic exists to fix. The size cost is real and accepted: rows grow as machines times days times projects. What keeps it off the render path is that the status line reads remote_window_costs alone — remote_day_costs is opened by ccreport, which is typed, not rendered per frame. Revisit if a machine's table passes a size worth measuring.

17. Reads scope to accounts.Timeline.uuid_at(now), not just writes, so a login switch cannot add a previous account's spend to this one's windows. The rows for that previous account stay: a switch back finds them without waiting for a pull, and a row nobody's read path selects costs storage alone. A stale row is therefore invisible rather than deleted, and the read-side filter is what makes that safe — it is not an optimisation and must not be dropped.

Out of scope here: the S and W quota segments, which are native per-account already and need none of this. Later: forecast.py reading the merged windows, and ccreport naming which machines a merged table covers.
acceptance: The status line's cost windows and ccreport -A show the account's spend across every pushing machine, correct within one push interval, with no record counted twice; a bare ccreport names the gap under each table; ccu is unchanged.
notes:
Related: ccreport-3soc (archive old ccreport_records into raw-identity day rows). No dependency edge either way; neither blocks the other.

Point 16 accepts unbounded growth in remote_day_costs and asks for a revisit once a machine's table passes a size worth measuring. ccreport-3soc is that revisit for the local half: on this machine 352,388 records older than 30 days fold to 3,329 rows at day grain, 106:1, taking cache.db from 214 MB toward 35 MB.

Two things to keep aligned when either is built:

- Grain. remote_day_costs is keyed on (server_url, account_uuid, machine_id, day, project). Give the local archive the same day, project and account columns so '-A' folds an archived local day and a pulled remote day through one path rather than two. Protocol version the push client and the server agree on
description:
`IngestBatch.client_version` is sent on every push and read by nobody;
`server_version()` is reported at `/health` and checked nowhere. Both read the
package version, which is `0.1.0` in pyproject.toml and has never been bumped —
this repo has no tags and no releases, master is the release and the unit is a
commit (see `ccreport update`). So neither side can tell whether the other
understands the payload it is being sent.

That already bites. The wire contract has grown three times recently:
`IngestBatch.extra` (the Extra-usage series), `IngestBatch.pull` /
`IngestResponse.pull` (the remainder), and `IngestResponse.extra`. A new client
posting any of those to an older server has them dropped by Pydantic and gets a
200 back, so `ccreport server push` reports success while the readings and the
remainder are silently lost. `ccreport server sync` on an old server stores no
remote costs at all and says nothing.

## What this needs

- A `PROTOCOL_VERSION` integer in one module, bumped by hand when the wire
  contract changes: a new payload section, a renamed field, a new response key.
  Deliberately NOT the package version and NOT the git sha — a refactor that
  moves no bytes on the wire must need no bump, and every commit differs from
  every other, which makes a sha advisory at best. Document the bump rule beside
  the constant and in AGENTS.md, the way MIGRATION_CHAIN's append-only rule is
  documented.
- The client sends it on every request (beside or instead of `client_version`,
  which stays useful as a human-readable build label). The server sends its own
  back on every response and at `/health`.
- Mismatch behaviour, decided:
  - **client protocol > server protocol**: the server answers 409 naming both
    numbers. The client treats it as terminal, the way it treats a 401 — a
    revoked token and an unusable server are both "stop, this will not fix
    itself on the next interval". `cache_db.write_push_attempt(..., stopped=True)`
    with the reason stored, so `ccreport server status` prints it.
  - **client protocol < server protocol**: the push proceeds. The server is
    newer and understands everything the client sends; there is nothing to lose.
    `ccreport server status` says the server is ahead and this machine should be
    updated.
  - equal: nothing is printed.
- `ccreport server connect` calls `/health` at setup, so a protocol mismatch has
  to fail there too rather than at the first push half an hour later.

## Files

- `src/ccreport/server/ingest.py` — `IngestBatch`, `IngestResponse`,
  `HealthResponse`, `server_version()`, the `/v1/ingest` and `/health` handlers.
- `src/ccreport/push.py` — `post_batch` (`_client_version`, the 401 terminal
  path at `PushError(terminal=True)`), `push_to`, `pull_from`.
- `src/ccreport/ccreport.py` — `cmd_server_status`, `cmd_server_connect`.
- `src/ccreport/cache_db.py` — the stored push outcome the status command reads.

Where the constant lives is an open question worth one minute of thought: it has
to be importable by both `push.py` (which must not import rich or FastAPI) and
`server/ingest.py`. A small module of its own, or an existing shared one.

Acceptance criteria:
- One `PROTOCOL_VERSION` constant, with the bump rule documented beside it and
  in AGENTS.md.
- Every ingest request carries it and every ingest response returns it;
  `/health` reports it.
- A client ahead of the server is refused with 409 and stops pushing, with the
  reason readable from `ccreport server status`.
- A client behind the server pushes normally and `ccreport server status` says
  the server is ahead.
- `ccreport server connect` fails at setup on a mismatch rather than at the
  first push.
- pytest covers all three directions (ahead, behind, equal) across ingest,
  health and connect; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

The -A gap note counted project names, not machines
description:
`ccreport monthly` on a machine with one pulled peer printed:

    Not shown: $14333 spent on this account from 48 other machine(s).

There is one other machine. `_remote_note` in `src/ccreport/ccreport.py` counted
`len({rec.project.split("/")[0] for rec in remote})`. That expression only names
a machine on a *redacted* row, where `reports.project_display` builds
`<machine>/aggregated`; on an ordinary row the prefix is the project name, so
the count was "distinct projects that machine pushed" — 48 of them.

Found while verifying ccreport-4x0s against the live server at
ccreport.lan.rykroken.net, after that epic had already been closed. The rest of
the epic verified correctly: -A totalled $29,488 = $15,155 local + $14,333
remote, and the status line merged its windows.

## Fix

`_remote_records` returns a `RemoteSpend` NamedTuple — the records plus the set
of machine labels that survived the same filters — instead of a bare list.
`_remote_note` reads `len(spend.machines)` and picks machine/machines rather
than printing "machine(s)". Callers updated: `_session_note` and the two places
in `main` that merge or note.

Acceptance criteria:
- The note counts machines. A test asserts one machine with several projects
  reads as one.
- `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

ccreport server disconnect: stop pushing to a server without editing push.toml
description:
`ccreport server connect` writes a server's entry into
`~/.config/ccreport/push.toml`; nothing takes one out again. Stopping means
editing the TOML by hand, and a person who does that leaves state behind that
the CLI has no other way to reach.

Seen live: `ccreport server status` on this machine lists
`http://oves-macbook-neo:8787` with 15 failed attempts in a row, beside the
server that actually works. Every detached push spawn still tries it, waits out
the connect timeout and stamps another failure.

## What is left behind by a hand edit

Removing the `[server."URL"]` table alone leaves five kinds of local state
keyed on that URL, none of which any other command clears:

- `push_state` rows — the per-file watermark (`cache_db.clear_push_state`).
- The per-server meta keys `_push_meta_key` builds: `samples_at`, `extra_at`,
  `policy`, the attempt stamp, the failure count, the terminal flag and the
  stored reason.
- `remote_window_costs` and `remote_day_costs` rows — and these are the ones
  that matter, because `-A` and the status line's merged cost windows keep
  adding a disconnected server's totals forever. A machine that stopped
  contributing goes on contributing.
- The `.restricted` marker beside push.toml, if this was the only restricted
  server. It deliberately outlives an edit to push.toml, so disconnecting the
  last restricted server must decide whether it goes.

## Shape

`ccreport server disconnect <url>` — the URL as push.toml spells it, and the
same "name the server when there is more than one" rule `_split_allow_targets`
already applies to `server allow`/`deny`.

- Print what will go: the entry, the row counts per table, and that the token's
  plaintext exists nowhere else, so reconnecting needs a token minted afresh in
  the web UI. That last point is the one a person cannot recover from.
- Confirm before doing it, `--yes` to skip, the way `cmd_adopt` does.
- Nothing is touched on the server. Its records, its machine row and its tokens
  stay; revoking or deleting the machine is the web UI's job, and which one to
  reach for is whether the machine is still out there.
- Leave the `.restricted` marker alone. It is a claim about this machine having
  been restricted, not about one server, and clearing it on a disconnect is how
  a later reconnect would read as open.

## Files

- `src/ccreport/push.py` — `read_raw`, `write_server` (a `remove_server`
  beside it, written the same way and at the same mode).
- `src/ccreport/cache_db.py` — `clear_push_state` clears part of this already;
  it needs a wider `forget_server(server_url)` that also takes the meta keys and
  the two remote cost tables.
- `src/ccreport/ccreport.py` — `cmd_server_disconnect`, the subparser, the
  dispatch in `main`.

Acceptance criteria:
- `ccreport server disconnect <url>` removes the entry and every local row keyed
  on that URL, behind a confirmation `--yes` skips.
- `ccreport -A` and the status line's merged windows stop counting that server's
  machines afterwards.
- Another configured server is left untouched.
- The `.restricted` marker survives.
- The output says a fresh token is needed to reconnect.
- pytest covers all of the above; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.

Settings pages count records without dedup: /settings/accounts shows 2.2x the real spend
description:
The /settings/accounts page reports far more spend than the dashboard for the same corpus. Observed on ccreport.lan.rykroken.net on 2026-08-19:

  account   | /settings/accounts | dashboard /
  personal  | $66,035.54         | $29,498.48
  work      | $13,421.44         |  $5,712.78

The dashboard all-time headline ($35,211.26) is the sum of its two deduped account figures, so the dashboard is right and the settings page is wrong by 2.24x and 2.35x.

Cause: db.account_overview (src/ccreport/server/db.py:520) sums with no dedup —

    SELECT r.account_uuid, COUNT(*), COALESCE(SUM(r.cost), 0), ...
      FROM server_records r
  GROUP BY r.account_uuid

while every other read path goes through reports._dedup_clause
(src/ccreport/server/reports.py:223), which keeps MIN(id) per
(account_uuid, dk) and passes through rows whose dk is NULL or empty. Two
machines that share session logs push the same call twice; the dashboard counts
it once, this page counts every copy. Both the Records column and the Cost
column are inflated.

db.machine_overview (src/ccreport/server/db.py:427) has the same shape: its
per-machine COUNT(*) over server_records is raw. Decide there whether a machine
row should report what it pushed (raw) or what survives the account-wide dedup —
the two answers differ and the column header should say which.
acceptance:
The Cost column on /settings/accounts equals the per-account figure the dashboard draws for the all-time range, for every account, on the production corpus.

The Records column counts deduped records, matching the calls the dashboard attributes to that account.

A record whose dk is NULL or empty is still counted once, as _dedup_clause does.

/settings/machines states which count it shows and is consistent with that statement.

A pytest test under tests/ seeds two machines pushing the same dedup key and asserts account_overview returns one copy of the cost.
notes:
Reuse the existing dedup rather than writing a second one: reports._dedup_clause already states it in SQL and is exercised by the dashboard on half a million records. account_overview groups by account with no filters, so it can bind an unfiltered Filters().

Watch the ordering: the query sorts by SUM(r.cost) DESC and that sum changes with the dedup.

description:
The /settings/accounts page reports far more spend than the dashboard for the same corpus. Observed on ccreport.lan.rykroken.net on 2026-08-19:

  account   | /settings/accounts | dashboard /
  personal  | $66,035.54         | $29,498.48
  work      | $13,421.44         |  $5,712.78

The dashboard all-time headline ($35,211.26) is the sum of its two deduped account figures, so the dashboard is right and the settings page is wrong by 2.24x and 2.35x.

Cause: db.account_overview (src/ccreport/server/db.py:520) sums with no dedup —

    SELECT r.account_uuid, COUNT(*), COALESCE(SUM(r.cost), 0), ...
      FROM server_records r
  GROUP BY r.account_uuid

while every other read path goes through reports._dedup_clause
(src/ccreport/server/reports.py:223), which keeps MIN(id) per
(account_uuid, dk) and passes through rows whose dk is NULL or empty. Two
machines that share session logs push the same call twice; the dashboard counts
it once, this page counts every copy. Both the Records column and the Cost
column are inflated.

db.machine_overview (src/ccreport/server/db.py:427) has the same shape: its
per-machine COUNT(*) over server_records is raw. Decide there whether a machine
row should report what it pushed (raw) or what survives the account-wide dedup —
the two answers differ and the column header should say which.
acceptance:
The Cost column on /settings/accounts equals the per-account figure the dashboard draws for the all-time range, for every account, on the production corpus.

The Records column counts deduped records, matching the calls the dashboard attributes to that account.

A record whose dk is NULL or empty is still counted once, as _dedup_clause does.

/settings/machines states which count it shows and is consistent with that statement.

A pytest test under tests/ seeds two machines pushing the same dedup key and asserts account_overview returns one copy of the cost.
notes:
Fixed on master (uncommitted at time of writing).

- reports.account_overview (src/ccreport/server/reports.py) is the deduped query; db.account_overview is gone. It could not stay in db.py: reports imports db, so the dedup cannot travel the other way.
- pages.accounts calls reports.account_overview.
- db.machine_overview keeps its raw COUNT(*); machines.html now heads the column "Pushed" and says what it counts.
- tests/test_server_reports.py::TestAccountOverview - six tests, including that the cost equals sum(reports.load(...)) per account and that a NULL dk is still counted.
- AGENTS.md records the invariant.

just lint-all and just test both pass: 2040 passed.

Not yet verified against the production corpus - the server runs from its own checkout and needs the deploy before /settings/accounts can be compared to the dashboard.
closed_reason: Deduped account_overview through reports._dedup_clause. Live /settings/accounts now reads $29,498.48 personal and $5,712.78 work, matching the dashboard to the cent (was $66,035.54 and $13,421.44). Machines page keeps the raw count under a Pushed header.

Resolve the account config across ~/.claude-config, ~/.claude and $HOME
description:
statusline._capture_account read a single hardcoded path, Path.home() / '.claude.json' (src/ccreport/statusline.py:871). Claude Code keeps the signed-in account under a config directory on some installs — ~/.claude/.claude.json exists on the user's Linux machine, ~/.claude.json on the macOS one — so on those installs no account event is ever recorded and every record stays unattributed.

Fix: _config_json_path() tries ~/.claude-config/.claude.json, then ~/.claude/.claude.json, then ~/.claude.json, first existing wins. The memo stamp gained the path so a file appearing in a config directory is not skipped as an unchanged rewrite.
acceptance: _config_json_path returns the first existing candidate in that order and the home file when none exist; _capture_account reads the resolved path; the memo skip is keyed on (path, mtime_ns, size); tests cover precedence and the stamp; just lint-all and just test pass.

title: Resolve the account config across ~/.claude-config, ~/.claude and $HOME
Backfill subscription tier history from billing receipts
description:
## Why

`account_events` is the only place a subscription tier is recorded, and a row
is written only when a status-line render notices the config blob changed. On
this machine that log starts months after the first record, so
`AccountTimeline.tier_at()` answers None for most of the corpus and
`ccreport limits` prints the tier as absent.

The plan history itself is recoverable from Stripe receipt emails: each one
names the line item in force for the period it covers, and an upgrade mid-cycle
bills a prorated line the same day it takes effect. So the receipt date is the
change moment and the line item is the plan.

Two further gaps make a local-only fix worth little:

- `server_records` carries no tier column, so the merged dashboard cannot show
  plan against spend even where the local log knows the answer.
- `account_events` is per machine, so every machine on an account needs the
  same backfill.

## Scope

1. A CLI command that writes `account_events` rows from a declared timeline —
   an accounts backfill subcommand reading a small TOML file of
   (timestamp, account, seat_tier, user_rate_limit_tier,
   organization_rate_limit_tier) entries. Idempotent: re-running with the same
   file writes nothing new. It must not invent identity — an entry names an
   account already present in the log and the command copies that identity
   forward, so a typo cannot split one account into two.
2. Carry the tier to the server: a `protocol.PROTOCOL_VERSION` bump, the tier on
   each pushed record (resolved client-side off `AccountTimeline`, the way the
   account label already is), a column on `server_records`, and a numbered
   `Step` appended to both `MIGRATION_CHAIN`s.
3. Surface it: the tier beside the account on the settings/accounts page, so a
   month's spend can be read against the plan that was paid for.

## Notes

- Tier strings observed so far: `default_claude_max_5x`,
  `default_claude_max_20x`, `default_raven`, seat `team_tier_1`. The string for
  the Pro plan is unverified — nothing in this repo carries it and no Claude
  Code bundle was available to grep. The command must accept whatever string
  the file gives rather than validating against a list.
- On a personal Max plan the tier lands in `organizationRateLimitTier` with
  `userRateLimitTier` null; on a Team seat both are set plus `seatTier`.
  `effective_limit_tier()` already resolves the pair and needs no change.
- Backfilled rows sort in by ts through the existing bisect in
  `AccountTimeline._index_at`, including alongside the ts=0 row `adopt` writes.
- `_ACCOUNT_IDENTITY_COLS` deliberately excludes the tiers, so extra rows that
  differ only in tier do not read as an account change.

## Acceptance criteria

- The backfill command writes one row per timeline entry and is a no-op on a
  second run against the same file.
- `ccreport limits` prints a tier for a window whose fill span predates the
  first captured event, once a backfill covers it.
- A pushed record carries its tier and the server stores it; a client older
  than the bump is refused, per the existing protocol rule.
- The settings/accounts page shows the tier in force.
- pytest coverage for the new command, the migration steps and the page.

title: Backfill subscription tier history from billing receipts
Backfill subscription tier history from billing receipts
description:
## Why

`account_events` is the only place a subscription tier is recorded, and a row
is written only when a status-line render notices the config blob changed. On a
machine whose capture started months after its first record,
`AccountTimeline.tier_at()` answers None for most of the corpus and
`ccreport limits` prints the tier as absent.

The plan history is recoverable from Stripe receipts: each names the line item
in force for the period it covers, and a mid-cycle upgrade bills a prorated
line the day it takes effect. So the receipt date is the change moment and the
line item is the plan.

The server has the same gap and cannot be fixed the same way. Its records reach
back further than any machine's logs do: `push.changed_files` offers only a file
whose (mtime_ns, size) moved and skips archived ones outright, so a per-record
tier pushed from a client would stamp recent history and leave the rest NULL
whatever `--full` does. The server therefore needs its own copy of the timeline,
resolved by timestamp the way `AccountTimeline` resolves one.

## Scope

### Client

1. An `account_events.source` column (`capture` | `backfill` | `adopt`), added
   by a numbered `Step` on `cache_db.MIGRATION_CHAIN`. It stays out of
   `_ACCOUNT_COLS`, so `record_account_event`'s identity comparison and
   `_ACCOUNT_SELECT` are untouched by it.
2. `read_latest_account()` selects `source = 'capture'` instead of
   `ts > ADOPTED_TS`. That is what it always meant, and it stops a backfilled
   row dated after the newest capture from becoming what `adopt` copies.
3. `ccreport accounts backfill <file.toml>` writes one row per declared entry
   through a new writer — `record_account_event` compares against the newest row
   alone and cannot take an out-of-order historic insert. Idempotent by
   `INSERT OR REPLACE` on ts. An entry names an account uuid already in the log
   and the command copies that identity forward, so a typo cannot split one
   account in two. Preview, then `_confirm`, with `--yes` to skip, as `cmd_adopt`
   does. `--remove` deletes `WHERE source = 'backfill'`.

### Server

4. An `account_tiers` table — (account_uuid, from_ts, seat_tier,
   user_rate_limit_tier, organization_rate_limit_tier, updated_at) — plus a bare
   `Step(N, "account_tiers")`, since the CREATE script covers a new table.
5. A timeline type in `reports.py` beside `account_display`, resolving a tier
   for a record's ts by bisect. Wired into the row builders so a folded row
   carries its tier.
6. `db.content_stamp` reads the table's count and max(updated_at): a tier typed
   in has no push behind it, exactly like `account_aliases`.
7. A settings page that takes the timeline as a textarea in the same TOML the
   CLI reads, so one declared file serves both ends, and replaces the account's
   rows wholesale.
8. The tier beside the account on the accounts settings page.

## Notes

- Tier strings observed: `default_claude_max_5x`, `default_claude_max_20x`,
  `default_raven`, seat `team_tier_1`. The Pro string is unverified — nothing in
  this repo carries it. Neither end may validate against a list.
- On a personal Max plan the tier lands in `organizationRateLimitTier` with
  `userRateLimitTier` null; on a team seat both are set plus `seatTier`.
  `effective_limit_tier()` already resolves the pair and needs no change.
- No protocol bump and no `server_records` migration: nothing new goes over the
  wire.
- Bumping `cache_db.SCHEMA_VERSION` moves `_ccreport_files_fingerprint` and
  re-parses the corpus once. Expected, not a defect.
- Every new event ts is a boundary `_plan_archive` holds a straddling file back
  on, and `_rollup_fingerprint` hashes the log whole, so rollups rebuild once
  after a backfill. Both are existing behaviour, worth asserting in tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- The backfill writes one row per entry, is a no-op on a second run against the
  same file, and `--remove` leaves only captured rows.
- `read_latest_account()` ignores a backfilled row newer than the newest capture.
- `ccreport limits` prints a tier for a window whose fill span predates the
  first captured event, once a backfill covers it.
- A server report groups spend by tier for records pushed before the tier
  existed anywhere.
- The accounts settings page shows the tier and accepts a pasted timeline.
- pytest coverage for the new command, both migration steps, the resolver and
  the page.

## Why

`ccreport limits` prints the tier as absent.

title: Backfill subscription tier history from billing receipts
Price a month against the plan that was paid for
description:
## Why

The declared plan timeline says which plan an account was on. Nothing says what
that plan cost, so the dashboard can show a month's API-price valuation with no
figure to set it against — which is the comparison the timeline was declared
for.

## Scope

1. `pricing.PLAN_PRICES`: monthly list prices per rate-limit tier, tax
   excluded, in the shape `PRICING_HISTORY` already uses — a list of periods
   each with an `effective` date and a tier-to-USD map — so a price rise is a
   new period rather than an edit to a shipped one. Prices live here and
   nowhere else, per the rule that all pricing data is in this file.
2. `pricing.plan_price(tier, when)`, resolving through those periods the way
   `find_pricing` resolves a model.
3. A month that held more than one plan is prorated by days in force, which is
   how a mid-cycle upgrade is actually billed. The split is two functions so
   neither module gains an import it may not have: `tier_timeline` turns
   entries into `(from_ts, to_ts, tier)` stretches bounded to a span — it
   imports nothing but the stdlib and must keep doing so — and `pricing` prices
   a list of stretches against the span.
4. A plan-cost column on the dashboard's `month` breakdown, beside the
   valuation already there. Summed across accounts on the whole-server page,
   one account's on an account page.

## Notes

- Tax is excluded on purpose. The list price is the same figure wherever the
  payer lives; a VAT rate is not, and a report that wants the money actually
  charged can apply one.
- A tier with no price is not zero. A month priced against one has to read as
  unpriced, the way a model with no price fails a file at ingest rather than
  storing a zero.
- The stretches come from the server's `account_tiers`, which is already read
  once per report and handed to the row builders.

## Acceptance criteria

- `plan_price` answers a tier at an instant and returns None for a tier it has
  no price for.
- A month wholly inside one plan prices as that plan's monthly rate.
- A month split across two plans prices as the two rates weighted by days.
- A month with no declared plan shows no figure rather than a zero.
- The column appears on the month breakdown and totals across accounts.
- pytest coverage for the price lookup, the stretches, the proration and the
  column.

Pull the declared plan timeline from the server
description:
## Why

The timeline now exists in four places — one file per machine plus the server's
`account_tiers` — and a plan change means editing every copy. They drift
silently: nothing compares them, and a machine left behind reports a stretch
under the wrong plan with no sign anything is wrong.

Making the server the one source removes three of the four copies. It is
already where the timeline has to be typed for the dashboard, and it is the
copy that reaches records no client can still re-push.

## Scope

1. Carry the declared timeline back on the ingest response, beside the cost
   rows `server/pull.py` already returns, rather than through `/v1/report`.
   That endpoint sits inside the network allowlist and answers nothing when a
   laptop is away from home, which is exactly when a machine is most likely to
   be running on a stale copy.
2. Bump `protocol.PROTOCOL_VERSION` to 2: a new section on the ingest response
   is the bump rule's first case.
3. Scope what comes back to `read_latest_account()`, as the remote cost tables
   already are, so a login switch cannot write another account's plan history
   into this machine's log.
4. Write the entries through `cache_db.backfill_account_events`, which is
   already keyed on ts and idempotent. A pull replaces the backfilled rows for
   the accounts the server declared and leaves captures alone.

## Notes

- `ccreport tiers <file>` stays. It is how a timeline is first written, how a
  machine that pushes to no server declares one, and what a person edits when
  the server is wrong.
- Decide and document which side wins when both have declared something for one
  account. Server-wins is the point of the change; it also means a local
  `ccreport tiers` run is undone by the next pull, and the command should say so.
- No new endpoint and no new round trip: `push.run_once` already pulls by
  default.

## Acceptance criteria

- An ingest response carries the asking machine's accounts' timelines.
- A pull writes them as backfilled rows and leaves captures untouched.
- A second pull with nothing changed writes nothing new.
- Another account's entries never reach a machine signed in elsewhere.
- A client one version behind still pushes; one ahead is refused, as now.
- pytest coverage for the response section, the write, and the account scoping.

Link each row on /settings/projects to that project's page
description:
The /settings/projects table lists every (machine, project) pair a machine has pushed, but the "Pushed as" cell is plain text. /settings/machines already links its machine_id cell, so the projects page is the odd one out — to see what a project actually cost you have to go back to the dashboard and find its row in the breakdown.

Make the project cell in src/ccreport/server/templates/projects.html:22 an anchor to the catch-all detail page, the same target the dashboard's breakdown builds in _breakdown_table.html:21:

    /project/{key}?days={days}

Two things decide the key:

1. It is the *displayed* name, not the pushed one. /{dimension}/{key} matches the string the breakdown table shows, which for a project is reports.project_display() — the project_aliases row for that (machine_id, project) pair if there is one, else the pushed name. project_overview() already returns both fields, so the link key is 'p.alias or p.project', urlencoded. Linking the raw p.project on an aliased row lands on a 404.
2. days is optional on the route (pages.py:456 defaults to dashboard.DEFAULT_RANGE), so the settings page can omit the query string entirely rather than invent a range.

A project name carries slashes, which is why the route declares {key:path} and why the alias form posts the pair in form fields — the urlencode filter in the href is what makes a slashed name reach the right page.

Files: src/ccreport/server/templates/projects.html, tests/test_pages.py (or wherever the /settings/projects test lives).
acceptance:
- Each row's "Pushed as" cell on /settings/projects is a link to /project/<displayed name>.
- On a row with an alias saved, the link uses the alias and the target page returns 200 with that project's rows.
- On a row with no alias, the link uses the pushed name.
- A project name containing a slash produces a link that resolves (urlencoded key against the {key:path} route).
- A test asserts the rendered href for both an aliased and an unaliased row.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

Show what the spend was worth against the plan that was paid for
description:
## Why

The month breakdown now carries a valuation and a plan cost side by side, and
the reader is left to divide them. The interesting figure — how many times over
the subscription paid for itself, and what that is in money — is the reason both
columns exist, so the page should state it.

title: Show what the spend was worth against the plan that was paid for
Price a month against the plan that was paid for
description:
## Why

The declared plan timeline says which plan an account was on. Nothing says what
that plan cost, so the dashboard can show a month's API-price valuation with no
figure to set it against — which is the comparison the timeline was declared
for.

## Scope

1. `pricing.PLAN_PRICES`: monthly list prices per rate-limit tier, tax
   excluded, in the shape `PRICING_HISTORY` already uses — a list of periods
   each with an `effective` date and a tier-to-USD map — so a price rise is a
   new period rather than an edit to a shipped one. Prices live here and
   nowhere else, per the rule that all pricing data is in this file.
2. `pricing.plan_price(tier, when)`, resolving through those periods the way
   `find_pricing` resolves a model.
3. A month that held more than one plan is prorated by days in force, which is
   how a mid-cycle upgrade is actually billed. The split is two functions so
   neither module gains an import it may not have: `tier_timeline` turns
   entries into `(from_ts, to_ts, tier)` stretches bounded to a span — it
   imports nothing but the stdlib and must keep doing so — and `pricing` prices
   a list of stretches against the span.
4. A plan-cost column on the dashboard's `month` breakdown, beside the
   valuation already there. Summed across accounts on the whole-server page,
   one account's on an account page.

## Notes

- Tax is excluded on purpose. The list price is the same figure wherever the
  payer lives; a VAT rate is not, and a report that wants the money actually
  charged can apply one.
- A tier with no price is not zero. A month priced against one has to read as
  unpriced, the way a model with no price fails a file at ingest rather than
  storing a zero.
- The stretches come from the server's `account_tiers`, which is already read
  once per report and handed to the row builders.

## Acceptance criteria

- `plan_price` answers a tier at an instant and returns None for a tier it has
  no price for.
- A month wholly inside one plan prices as that plan's monthly rate.
- A month split across two plans prices as the two rates weighted by days.
- A month with no declared plan shows no figure rather than a zero.
- The column appears on the month breakdown and totals across accounts.
- pytest coverage for the price lookup, the stretches, the proration and the
  column.
closed_reason: Plan prices in pricing.py, prorated month column on the dashboard

Link each row on /settings/projects to that project's page
description:
The /settings/projects table lists every (machine, project) pair a machine has pushed, but the "Pushed as" cell is plain text. /settings/machines already links its machine_id cell, so the projects page is the odd one out — to see what a project actually cost you have to go back to the dashboard and find its row in the breakdown.

Make the project cell in src/ccreport/server/templates/projects.html:22 an anchor to the catch-all detail page, the same target the dashboard's breakdown builds in _breakdown_table.html:21:

    /project/{key}?days={days}

Two things decide the key:

1. It is the *displayed* name, not the pushed one. /{dimension}/{key} matches the string the breakdown table shows, which for a project is reports.project_display() — the project_aliases row for that (machine_id, project) pair if there is one, else the pushed name. project_overview() already returns both fields, so the link key is 'p.alias or p.project', urlencoded. Linking the raw p.project on an aliased row lands on a 404.
2. days is optional on the route (pages.py:456 defaults to dashboard.DEFAULT_RANGE), so the settings page can omit the query string entirely rather than invent a range.

A project name carries slashes, which is why the route declares {key:path} and why the alias form posts the pair in form fields — the urlencode filter in the href is what makes a slashed name reach the right page.

Files: src/ccreport/server/templates/projects.html, tests/test_pages.py (or wherever the /settings/projects test lives).
acceptance:
- Each row's "Pushed as" cell on /settings/projects is a link to /project/<displayed name>.
- On a row with an alias saved, the link uses the alias and the target page returns 200 with that project's rows.
- On a row with no alias, the link uses the pushed name.
- A project name containing a slash produces a link that resolves (urlencoded key against the {key:path} route).
- A test asserts the rendered href for both an aliased and an unaliased row.
- just lint-all and just test pass.
